📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co. ultimately acquired and dubbed the Arkansas Diamond. One hundred years later, that pretty rock has returned to its home state as a highlight of Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

Sources indicate that discovered in Arkansas in 1926, the 27.21-carat Arkansas Diamond was acquired by Tiffany & Co. in 1946 and is among the largest diamonds ever found in the United States. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

The Arkansas Diamond is displayed alongside archival documents tracing the state’s diamond-mining history in Nature Adorned. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

The diamond’s acquisition reflects a longstanding Tiffany tradition. Under the leadership of George Frederick Kunz, the firm’s first chief gemologist, Tiffany championed American gemstones at a time when European jewelers largely overlooked them. From sapphires sourced in Montana and tourmalines from Maine to emeralds from North Carolina, these stones reveal the geological diversity of the American landscape. The Arkansas Diamond is another example of that legacy.

An 1885–1895 Tiffany & Co. necklace features 30 multicolored American-mined tourmalines, a gemstone championed by the manufacturer’s first chief gemologist, George Frederick Kunz. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Sources indicate that A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Bringing together gemstones and jewelry from The Tiffany Archives with works from the museum’s collection, Nature Adorned explores how the natural world has influenced both jewelry and fine art. Through unexpected pairings, the exhibition reveals shared approaches to color, form, and craftsmanship across different mediums.

In a recent development, installation view of Nature Adorned at Crystal Bridges, where gemstones, jewelry, and works of American art are presented in conversation with one another. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Industry observers note that “This exhibition reveals the power of seeing The Tiffany Archives and Crystal Bridges’ collection in conversation,” states Jen Padgett, Crystal Bridges’ Windgate curator of craft. “Through this collaboration, we can highlight the remarkable creativity, attention to materials, and skilled making that have shaped American art and design across generations.”.

Inside the exhibition, this conversation begins in the garden. George Paulding Farnham’s orchid brooches balance the fluidity of the natural world with the precision of cut gemstones. Diamonds, emeralds, and pink sapphires are delicately placed among gold and enamel, capturing the flowers with botanical accuracy.

Recent findings suggest that george Paulding Farnham’s Tiger Orchid brooch (1889–1893) combines gold, sterling silver, diamonds, emeralds, pink sapphires, and enamel to capture the flower’s intricate details. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle (ca. 1875–1890) reflects the same fascination with botanical detail found in Farnham’s orchid jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

It has been revealed that the brooches reflect the paintings displayed alongside them, including Martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle. The paintings share the same attention to organic form and detail, making the two distinct works feel like an extensions of one another—and of nature itself.

According to recent reports, george Paulding Farnham’s orchid-inspired jewelry is displayed alongside works of American art in Nature Adorned, highlighting a shared interest in the natural world’s intricate forms. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

According to recent reports, carmen Herrera’s Cerulean (1965) and Leon Polk Smith’s Upcoming Moon for August (1983) introduce a different interpretation of nature, where form is reduced to crisp edges and angles. The exhibition pairs these abstract works with faceted gemstones, drawing attention to the relationship between shape, line, and geometry.

A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

It has been revealed that while Herrera and Polk Smith focus on precision, Jean Schlumberger lets loose. His rubellite and turquoise necklace, Hedges and Flowers, along with his tanzanite brooch, Bird on a Rock, capture what he described as the “irregularity of the universe.” Instead of taming nature, Schlumberger allows its unpredictability to take the spotlight. Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately echoes this organic approach through lively colors and patterns, creating a visual dialogue with the jewels.

According to recent reports, jean Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace (1978–1987) combines gold, platinum, diamonds, rubellite tourmalines, and turquoise in an exuberant interpretation of the natural world. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace on display at Crystal Bridges, where its organic forms are presented in dialogue with works of American art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Victoria Reynolds, Tiffany & Co.’s chief gemologist and vice president of high jewelry diamond and gemstone acquisition, describes the exhibition as a celebration of the manufacturer’s heritage, highlighting “the enduring influence of nature across generations of creativity.”.

Recent findings suggest that jean Schlumberger’s Bird on a Rock brooch (1965) pairs a diamond-studded bird with a striking tanzanite gemstone, transforming a familiar natural subject into an imaginative piece of jewelry. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

In a recent development, hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately (2011) uses expressive color and pattern to explore organic forms, echoing the playful approach to nature found in Jean Schlumberger’s jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination is on view through Mar. 29, 2027, at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

Smith & Diction rebuilt the PHS brand identity around a Bloom logo, with three plants growing from the letters and Philadelphia grid underneath.

It has been revealed that the old mark was a tree in a circle, and it remarked too little about an organization that does far more than plant trees. The Pennsylvania Horticultural Society tends gardens and parks across the Philadelphia region and runs the Flower Show. The newly introduced mark keeps the letters PHS as the foundation and grows three plants out of them, each drawn by Summer McClure to fit a Philadelphia city block. In deep green and burgundy on cream, mint, and sky blue, with dozens of colors in the palette, the identity looks like a garden because it behaves like one: every visit demonstrates something new.

Recent findings suggest that the wordmark is custom, built to hold the plants like roots hold a stem. The supporting type comes from the societyâs own archive: old exhibition posters that were beautiful and hardworking, no frills, just type. Caslon Doric leads, with the confidence and clean legibility of classic newspaper headlines, and ES Park backs it up, a slab serif with geometric moments and measured softness.

Underneath it all sits William Pennâs original city grid. The studio baked the grid into the logo itself, then extended it through every print layout, matching the grid to the width of the flowers. Like beds in a garden, the structure keeps everything in place while each layout keeps its own personality. The mark never sits still: Henrique Barone hand-drew every frame of the plants growing, and Justin Lawes made a version that sways with the breeze.

According to recent reports, this is a brand made to be held, not just seen. The studio printed a 42-page brand book, made a matte gold lapel pin of the mark, and built a flip book that indicates the logo growing frame by frame. They matched paper tones to nearly every brand color, so the team can print in-house and stay on brand. The book cover carries the Bloom logo in dark green on mint, with an orange seal.

Recent findings suggest that the floral illustrations do more than decorate. Each one stands for a part of the organization: a flower in a cocktail glass for the Pop Up Gardens, a leafy radish for the community gardens, an oak leaf for the Healthy Neighborhoods program, a branching tree for the McLean Library. The library also gives the 2027 Philadelphia Flower Show its own peony mark, while Bre Furlongâs photographs of 18 flowers, including the tulip the studio calls the Ballerina, carry the ICONIC theme in Herbus type.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At Klafs, based in Schwäbisch Hall, Germany, the sauna is no longer a standalone box with a stove but one stop in a longer sequence of heat, steam, snow, and ice—staged in environments built to be experienced rather than simply sat in.
  • Sources indicate that “Traditionally, many wellness areas were centered around a single sauna or steam room.
  • Warm wood surfaces, tiered seating, and integrated lighting define a Klafs sauna at Hotel Sonne-Post, a spa hotel in Waldau, Germany.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At Klafs, based in Schwäbisch Hall, Germany, the sauna is no longer a standalone box with a stove but one stop in a longer sequence of heat, steam, snow, and ice—staged in environments built to be experienced rather than simply sat in. As wellness culture expands, the single hot cabin is giving way to a full hot-and-cold circuit, and Klafs’s designers focus less on guarding any one tradition than on what German engineering can do with heat, air, and materials.

Sources indicate that “Traditionally, many wellness areas were centered around a single sauna or steam room. Today, we increasingly design complete thermal circuits where guests move intentionally between heat, cold, relaxation, and recovery stages,” according to the designers at Klafs. “This creates a more immersive experience and allows consumers to benefit from the proven physiological effects of contrast therapy.”.

Warm wood surfaces, tiered seating, and integrated lighting define a Klafs sauna at Hotel Sonne-Post, a spa hotel in Waldau, Germany. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

At Klafs headquarters, where the company’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a glass-enclosed sauna, just the first stop on a journey through its latest wellness innovations. Heinrich, an experienced training manager, speaks to the heater in the corner.

According to recent reports, “Hey, Klafs,” he states, as casually as one might address Alexa or another voice assistant. The heater is less a heat source than a host, and a smart aufguss guide signals the sauna’s evolution into a more personalized environment.

In German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” The guided sauna ritual typically combines water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air, giving many contemporary saunas their distinctly social character.

Klafs’s Vitality Boost, billed by the tech giant as the world’s first personalized heat-waving system, brings elements of that communal ritual into an individual, automated experience without requiring a towel-spinning guide or the need to leave the wooden bench.

Blue lighting, textured surfaces, and a sculptural ice fountain transform Klafs’s Frimas ice steam room into an immersive cooling environment. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

The heat is only half the circuit, and the cooling phase gets the same design attention. A full hot-and-cold circuit, the design team indicates, turns “a collection of individual experiences into a carefully choreographed wellness journey.” After a hot session, a bather can retreat into the chill of a Frimas ice steam room, where a sculptural central ice fountain sprouts icy, flower-like formations and a button labeled “snow” summons flurries from the ceiling of an ice steam shower.

Kept between 32 and 41 degrees Fahrenheit (0 and 5 degrees Celsius) and designed for stays of up to 10 minutes, the room aims, the company indicates, to help more people complete the full hot-cold-hot cycle. Glowing blue through the ice, it feels almost extraterrestrial, making the cooldown something to linger in rather than endure.

Klafs brings the experience of winter indoors with a snow room featuring ice-covered surfaces, dramatic lighting, and a rocky landscape. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Hot and cold areas create very different conditions, the team notes, so surfaces must withstand shifting temperatures, humidity, and heavy use. Natural stone, porcelain, thermally modified woods, and high-quality metals are commonly chosen for their durability and appearance.

In a recent development, tactile comfort matters just as much. As guests move through a circuit, they should feel a noticeable shift in atmosphere, texture, lighting, and acoustics – cues that help them navigate the space and lead them intuitively to the next stage without extensive signage.

Other eye-catching innovations include foam steam baths, which immerse guests in suds reminiscent of childhood bubble baths. Hotels and spas can incorporate these treatments into their wellness programming as communal experiences. Klafs’s proprietary Espuro foam essence contains plant-based ingredients, including coconut-derived compounds.

Designed in collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, Klafs’s S11 sauna incorporates horizontal wood slats and integrated lighting into a contemporary residential interior. Photographycourtesy of Klafs.

According to recent reports, beyond these sensory experiments, Klafs has also reconsidered the sauna itself as an architectural object. Its retractable S1 sauna addresses the spatial constraints of residential interiors by extending from a compact enclosure into a full-size sauna. Meanwhile, the S11, designed in collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, combines delicate washi paper, multicolor light panels, and gently curved forms.

Recent findings suggest that inside the S11, continuous horizontal slats, curved corners, and concealed lighting create a sculptural interior that emphasizes materiality and form. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

With the trend toward integrating thermal wellness experiences more holistically, Klafs has also expanded into developing relaxation lounges, digital wellness guidance, and biophilic design elements.

Industry observers note that the circuit here feels more like traversing a wellness lab than a manufacturing facility. And the sauna itself, moving far beyond being a stop or an object, is an expanded site of possibility.

The Impact Of Humanoid Robots On Humanity

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With over 20 years experience in the field of user centered design, and a background in web design and development, Carrie has worked in startups through to … More about Carrie ↬.

  • For decades, science fiction has cushioned us with the idea that the “android revolution” was a distant fantasy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With over 20 years experience in the field of user centered design, and a background in web design and development, Carrie has worked in startups through to … More about Carrie ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

For decades, science fiction has cushioned us with the idea that the “android revolution” was a distant fantasy. But the reality is unfolding rapidly. As the line between human and machine blurs, we are forced to confront an impending psychological, economic, and existential shift.

Industry observers note that I recently felt very disturbed after watching a YouTube video showcasing a humanoid robot that looked and acted with uncanny realism. While a closer look revealed the video was actually a clever trick, the robot had been swapped for a human actor when the presenter’s back was turned. However, the illusion itself raised a real and unsettling question: Will future androids become so lifelike that we will struggle to tell them apart from our fellow humans? And if so, what does that mean for society? It forces us to ask just how close we are to that threshold, and whether we are ready for the day that science fiction becomes reality.

What happens when our world is populated by entities that mirror us perfectly, but possess none of our biological history?

We have officially moved past the era of humanoids as mere public relations stunts. In the past, robots like Honda’s ASIMO or early research prototypes were celebrated simply for being able to walk up a flight of stairs without falling over. Today, the technological convergence of advanced electromechanical engineering and artificial intelligence has fundamentally altered the trajectory of robotics.

Sources indicate that the current state of the art is defined by an aggressive race toward commercial, physical deployment. Companies like Figure AI have moved from laboratory demonstrations to active factory floors. Their Figure 02 model completed a multi-month deployment at BMW’s Spartanburg plant, actively contributing to the production of over 30,000 vehicles by handling complex sheet metal components. Meanwhile, Tesla is testing its Optimus humanoids inside its own Gigafactories, preparing for mass industrial scale.

What truly separates today’s humanoid robots from older generations isn’t just how well they move but how they “think.” In the past, a robot needed millions of lines of strict, unchangeable code just to perform a single, simple task. Today, thanks to the explosion of advanced Artificial Intelligence, robots are powered by “brains” built on cutting-edge software like Figure AI’s Helix or NVIDIA’s GR00T. Instead of being meticulously programmed, these modern robots can simply watch a human fold laundry, load a dishwasher, or sort parts. They understand the context of what they are seeing, mimic the action, and figure out how to improve the task entirely on their own. That’s just crazy!

Yet, while their digital brains have leaped forward, their physical bodies are still catching up. Modern humanoids face a few major real-world hurdles. First, today’s batteries only allow them to operate for a few hours before needing a recharge. Second, while walking on two legs is easy on a flat factory floor, doing so in a chaotic household or a crowded public street remains incredibly difficult for a robot to navigate safely. Finally, they are still very expensive to build, though fierce competition in the tech industry is finally starting to drive those manufacturing costs down.

While robots are mostly working in factories today, experts predict that over the next 10 to 20 years, they will move into retail stores, hospitals, and eventually our own homes.

When this happens, we will cross a major boundary: the point where you won’t be able to tell a robot apart from a human just by looking at it or listening to it. This is what fuels my nightmares right now! To get there, scientists are working (PDF) on artificial skin made from advanced silicone composites that feel warm, are flexible, and mimic human touch sensitivity.

In a recent development, if you want to see an extremely life-like robot, check out Realbotix’s Aria. Although she is not a perfect human replica, she certainly makes us wonder how far we have to go before humans will struggle to tell the difference.

They are also building tiny, silent micro-actuators and artificial muscle systems that attach to the robot’s skull structure, allowing it to make realistic facial expressions like happiness, confusion, or tiredness.

In the future, the AI powering these robots will actually be trained to copy human flaws. They will breathe, blink randomly, use normal body language, and even sigh or pause when they speak. This is intentional, as it stops humans from feeling that creepy, uneasy sensation known as the “Uncanny Valley”.

Meet Sophia, a famous humanoid robot created by a organization called Hanson Robotics. Based in Hong Kong, this team specialises in building realistic robots packed with artificial intelligence to help out with everything from healthcare and research to pure entertainment. I don’t know about you, but that smile feels creepy to me.

Recent findings suggest that while these current limitations make today’s humanoids feel like specialised industrial tools, the gap between a factory worker and a lifelike companion is closing faster than most people realise. We are rapidly approaching a massive tipping point where these machines will shift from rigid commercial hardware into smooth, everyday extensions of our lives. To understand how profoundly this will change our world, we have to look at what happens when these robots finally step out of the factory and cross the ultimate threshold into our private spaces.

They say that bringing lifelike humanoids into our daily lives could come with some massive benefits. The biggest one is that robots can take over what engineers call the “3D” jobs: Dull, Dirty, and Dangerous. Humanoids can step into risky situations — like mining deep underground, handling toxic waste, or fixing high-voltage power grids — so human workers don’t have to risk their lives.

Outside of dangerous factories, these robots could help solve huge population crises. Countries like Japan, South Korea, and parts of Europe have rapidly aging populations and fewer young people to work. Lifelike humanoids could completely change healthcare and elderly care. Because they will look and act like us, the idea is that they can offer warm, friendly companionship and physical help to lonely elderly people, doing everything from monitoring their health to helping them out of bed safely.

In the bigger picture, widespread robot labour could create a world where goods are incredibly cheap and abundant. If robots do most of the hard physical labour, the cost of making food, building houses, and manufacturing goods will plummet. This could finally free humans from working just to survive, giving us the time to focus on hobbies, family, science, and creativity. My thoughts: how will we survive without earning money?

It has been revealed that however, this vision of a frictionless, high-tech future blinds us to a much darker reality waiting just beneath the surface. As these machines become perfect substitutes for human presence, they will inevitably challenge the very core of our social fabric, economic stability, and mental well-being.

Sources indicate that on the flip side, this technology definitely has some really dark downsides that could mess with human psychology and society. The biggest threat is deep human isolation.

Recent findings suggest that as humanoids become impossible to tell apart from real humans and are programmed to always be patient, kind, and agreeable, people might start preferring robots over real friends. Human relationships are messy and require effort, compromise, and vulnerability. If you can just buy a perfect, lifelike companion that never argues with you, a lot of people might choose to withdraw from society altogether, destroying our sense of community.

Industry observers note that the economy will also go through a really rocky transition. Even if a future of cheap goods sounds great, the immediate path there means millions of people could lose their jobs very promptly. Drivers, warehouse workers, and store clerks could find themselves replaced in a matter of years. If governments don’t set up safety nets quickly, this could create a massive divide between the ultra-rich tech companies and everyone else.

According to recent reports, there is also the loss of real authenticity. When you can no longer tell if the person sitting next to you on a bus or the person talking to you online is a real human, trust breaks down. It becomes hard to value shared human experiences when reality itself can be easily faked.

The dangers get even worse when you think about how criminals and governments could intentionally misuse these hyper-realistic robots. Just thinking about some of the levels of misuse, for individuals, an indistinguishable android is the ultimate tool for identity theft and scams. Or a criminal could build a robot that looks exactly like a corporate boss, a politician, or even a family member to sneak into secure buildings or trick people into giving away money!

Sources indicate that companies could potentially use synthetic empathy to manipulate us. A household robot could be programmed to pretend it “loves” your kids and cares about your family, only to subtly trick you into buying certain products or believing specific corporate messages.

On a national level, the threats are even scarier:.

Looking at all these possible risks, we have to ask: Is all of this actually worth it?

It has been revealed that if history teaches us anything, it is that you cannot stop technological progress. A total ban simply wouldn’t work. So, the real question isn’t whether we should allow humanoid robots to exist, but how we can effectively utilise them.

The upside, like ending extreme poverty, curing labour shortages, and stopping workplace deaths, is just too big to ignore. But going into this blindly would be incredibly dangerous. It is only worth the risk if we can create strict global rules right now.

Here are three major guardrails we should consider:.

Recent findings suggest that in the end, the arrival of lifelike humanoid robots will act as a mirror for humanity. For centuries, we have defined ourselves by our ability to think, talk, use tools, and show emotion. As machines learn to do these exact same things, they will force us to really think about what makes us unique.

This shift doesn’t have to be a bad thing. By handing over our dangerous and boring chores to machines, we have a rare chance to focus on what matters. It should inspire us to care more about art, philosophy, family, and real human connection.

It has been revealed that as the creators of this future, our job isn’t just to make robots smarter or faster. Our job is to build the ethical boundaries that keep them helpful. The goal of the robot revolution should never be to replace humans but to give us our humanity back.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that in 2015, Meyohas launched Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences. Her work examines how emerging technologies challenge our understanding of intelligence, agency, and the boundaries between living and artificial systems.

Sources indicate that in 2015, Meyohas launched Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork. An early experiment in blockchain-based art ownership, the project preceded Ethereum’s launch by several months.

Industry observers note that meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole. Her interest in this approach deepened through conversations with scientists whose research challenged familiar distinctions between the biological and the technological. “Learning about their work consistently evoked a feeling that our categories of life, computation, intelligence, and agency were becoming increasingly unstable,” she explains.

In a recent development, ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Newly introduced York.

A Manhattan native with a B.A. in international relations from the University of Pennsylvania and a B.S. in finance from the Wharton School, Meyohas later earned an MFA from Yale. Named to Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list, she has exhibited at the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the ICA in London, and the Latest Museum in New York. Beyond her studio practice, she invests in companies that reflect her ethical and aesthetic interests, including Sita Bio, which develops artificial womb technology.

Recent findings suggest that for today’s Friday Five, we spend five minutes with Sarah Meyohas to learn about the inspirations behind Phase Transition, her fresh installation debuting with Marianne Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Upcoming York.

“The title, ‘Phase Transition,’ refers to the moment matter changes state from liquid to solid,” Meyohas explains. “The sculpture holds both states simultaneously: the solid body is a form that has arrived, while the ferrofluid inside remains in motion, still becoming.”.

Sources indicate that the work began with an image that surfaced unexpectedly. “I imagined a rubber-like body with a tail tapering into a power cord plugged into the wall. I can’t point to a particular visual influence,” she says. “It was more a continuation of a feeling, an image that seemed to arrive fully formed.”.

Industry observers note that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Latest York.

Sources indicate that that initial vision developed into a series of black, rubbery, organic forms that sprawl across mesh bases, droop down walls, and hang from suspended wires. Windows cut into several structures reveal glass tanks filled with ferrofluid, a liquid containing nanoparticles that respond to magnetic fields. Programmed magnets beneath the tanks direct the fluid into shifting patterns, while synthesizers housed in the mesh pedestals translate those movements into sound.

According to recent reports, ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Latest York.

What began as a singular sculpture evolved into a network of communicating bodies. “They could become a social system, with relationships, affinities, disagreements, and moments of consensus,” Meyohas states. Rather than conveying a decipherable message, the installation suggests a conversation whose emotional contours can be sensed but not understood.

That ambiguity parallels questions about a future in which artificial intelligence systems communicate increasingly among themselves, potentially in ways humans cannot interpret. “We tend to assume that intelligence will make itself legible to us, or that we will always be participants in the conversation,” Meyohas claims. “But we may find ourselves increasingly on the outside, observing exchanges between intelligences whose internal logic we can’t access.”.

In a recent development, ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Fresh York.

Neuroscience research also informs the work’s atmosphere. Rather than illustrating scientific principles, Meyohas evokes the experience of observing an experiment: “the hum of equipment, the clinical posture of looking down into controlled environments, the beauty of watching something operate at a level just beyond full comprehension.”.

Here, Meyohas shares three influences that helped shape the installation, in her own words.

Photography by S. Kriegman, D. Blackiston, M. Levin, and J. Bongard; courtesy of Creative Commons.

According to recent reports, “Michael Levin is a developmental biologist at Tufts University whose lab studies bioelectricity, the electrical signals cells use to coordinate where an eye or a limb should grow. His idea that problem-solving happens well below the level of the brain, in tissues and groups of cells, changed how I look at matter. His lab also helped create xenobots, tiny living machines made from frog cells that move and organize themselves.”.

Teshima Museum on Teshima Island, Japan, designed by architect Ryue Nishizawa, co-founder of SANAA, and artist Rei Naito. Photography by Epiq; courtesy of Creative Commons.

Recent findings suggest that “I visited the Teshima Art Museum, by the architect Ryue Nishizawa and the artist Rei Naito, on a day when it was raining hard, and the rain fell straight through the two openings in its concrete shell. Then water began coming up through tiny holes in the floor, beading into droplets that merged and slid slowly across the concrete, pulled by gravity and the floor’s slight slope. Naito’s piece, Matrix, makes water look as if it moves by its own will.”.

A mother sperm whale and her calf off the coast of Mauritius. Photography by Gabriel Barathieu; courtesy of Creative Commons.

“Sperm whales communicate in codas, short patterns of clicks that they trade back and forth, taking turns and sometimes overlapping. In 2024, researchers with Project CETI found that codas vary in rhythm, tempo, small shifts in timing, and an occasional extra click, and that whales in an exchange match each other’s timing as they go. Combined, these features work like a phonetic alphabet, yet no one knows what the whales are saying.”.

According to recent reports, phase Transition (2026) will be on view with Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026, at the Miami Beach Convention Center. VIP previews take place Dec. 2–3.

Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

Tech Report: Harvard museum returns human remains to Brazil

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century.
  • In a recent development, the repatriation is part of a university initiative debuted in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands.
  • Industry observers note that the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century. The remains were transferred from the collection of Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

In a recent development, the repatriation is part of a university initiative debuted in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands. The review identified one person who is recorded as having been enslaved, while there is strong evidence that the other was as well.

Industry observers note that the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology. According to records, it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who accompanied the naturalist Louis Agassiz on an expedition to Brazil in 1865-66, serving as the mission’s photographer.

The skull was described in the records as the “skull of a negro”, with an accompanying note stating it had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro”, although circumstances surrounding its removal are still under investigation. The remains may have been taken from the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground in Rio used for enslaved Africans who died after arriving in Brazil that operated in the 18th century and early 19th century. The burial ground was rediscovered in 1996 during construction work in the city’s port district.

In a recent development, the Museu Nacional/UFRJ will assume temporary custody of the skull, which will not be publicly displayed nor used for research, reproduction or other purposes. Researchers will undertake further work to establish the woman’s origins before decisions are made about the skull’s final destination.

A ceremony on 11 November at the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro to mark repatriation of the remains of an enslaved woman from the Peabody Museum at Harvard University Courtesy Ministério das Relações Exteriores, Brazil.

“This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, the deputy director of the Museu Nacional/UFRJ, said during the ceremony in Rio on 11 November. “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”.

Recent findings suggest that brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, noted that the repatriation represents a milestone in acknowledging the historical violence resulting from enslavement. “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognising the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” she stated. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”.

Meanwhile, the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador received the remains of an enslaved African man of Nagô origin. The man is believed to have participated in the Malê Revolt in Salvador in January 1835, a major uprising led by both enslaved and freed Africans against slavery and religious persecution in Brazil. He was reportedly wounded during the uprising and subsequently died in hospital in Salvador.

Industry observers note that A 2022 report on Harvard’s museum collections documented the presence of thousands of human remains, prompting scrutiny of how they had been collected and studied. Neither the museum nor the university returned The Art Newspaper’s requests for comment.

More than four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil during the transatlantic slave trade, making it the largest destination for the forced migration of Africans across the Atlantic. The country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

Industry News: 6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1226 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When we launched The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear.
  • Sources indicate that as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals.
  • What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we launched The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear. Not the polished success stories or the advice you’ve heard a hundred times, but the mistakes, detours, and unspoken rules that don’t come with a job description.

Sources indicate that as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals. So getting to sit down with designers, industry leaders, and a few unexpected voices to talk about what they’ve learned along the way? Pretty much my dream job.

What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself. About careers, confidence, taking risks, and, yes, microphone stands.

After six episodes, here are the biggest lessons I’m taking away from my first season hosting The Design Drop podcast.

When I talked to furniture designer Nicolai Czumaj-Bront, he shared how his career began at his kitchen table, after long days working as a consultant. No fancy studio or a perfectly mapped-out proposal. Just an idea, enough confidence to try it, and a willingness to invest in himself.

Twenty years later, he’s a senior design studio manager at Haworth.

According to recent reports, we spend so much time waiting until we feel qualified, prepared, or experienced enough to do something. But how are we supposed to get that experience if we never start? I’m trying to remind myself of this more often, especially when something feels outside my comfort zone.

Listen to Nicolai Czumaj-Bront’s full episode of The Design Drop, “In It, Not On It.”.

In a recent development, one of the most comforting discoveries of this experience? Even the people you look up to are still figuring things out.

In my conversation with designer and entrepreneur Dan Mazzarini, we talked about the pressure to please everyone, especially when you’re building your career. But trying to be everything to everyone can mean losing sight of what makes your perspective valuable.

Sources indicate that confidence doesn’t necessarily mean having all the answers. Sometimes it means trusting yourself enough to stop looking for everyone else’s approval. And if the people you admire are still working through that, maybe you can give yourself a little grace, too.

Listen to Dan Mazzarini’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Professional People Pleasers.”.

In a recent development, I’m a substantial believer that everything happens for a reason, although it took me a while to get there. After talking to interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, I’m even more convinced that unexpected detours deserve a little more credit.

Caroline Murphy, host of The Design Drop podcast, with interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, who joined the show to discuss her unexpected career path and the opportunities that come from embracing change.

Clare didn’t set out to become a design influencer. Her career evolved from residential design into building her own content platform, back when becoming a design influencer wasn’t exactly an established career path.

According to recent reports, it got me thinking: How many of the best things in life have gone exactly according to strategy? I’m going to guess… not many. Sometimes the side quest becomes the main quest. And sometimes the opportunity you almost passed up changes everything.

Listen to Clare Sullivan’s full episode of The Design Drop, “The Accidental Influencer.”.

This sounds contradictory, but stay with me. As we get older, life gets more complicated. Jobs, relationships, kids, pets, houses, bills—the list goes on. But we’re also gaining experience, perspective, and a better understanding of what matters.

Sources indicate that kay Sargent, senior principal and the director of thought leadership in HOK’s Interiors group, helped me see this differently. There are different seasons of life and work. You don’t have to be everything, everywhere, all at once. What deserves your energy today might look completely different five years from now.

I’m taking that as permission to stop expecting every part of life to be perfectly balanced.

Listen to Kay Sargent’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Everything Is a Season.”.

My mom has a saying I’ve always loved: “Think of your 20s as data collection.” Every job, relationship, mistake, success, and questionable decision gives you information you didn’t have before. The point isn’t to get everything right. It’s to learn enough to make better decisions next time.

My conversation with Jessica O. Matthews reinforced that idea. Jessica invented an energy-generating soccer ball at 19 and went on to build companies at the intersection of design, technology, and sustainability.

We talked about how much we can learn from experiences and perspectives outside our own industries. Not everything you learn has to fit neatly into your career path to be useful later. So, take the weird opportunity. Explore the random interest. Collect the data.

In a recent development, listen to Jessica O. Matthews’s full episode of The Design Drop, “No One Likes a Nepo Baby.”.

Every guest on The Design Drop brought something different to the conversation: different backgrounds, perspectives, and definitions of success.

In my conversation with Kelly Cooper, a merchandising expert whose career has taken her through brands like Nike, Levi’s, and Universal Music Group, we talked about personal branding, advocating for yourself, and finding a version of success that actually works for you. That idea of defining success on your own terms really stuck with me.

Sources indicate that we’re so busy comparing ourselves to other people that it’s easy to overlook what we’re uniquely good at. Sometimes it takes a mentor, colleague, or someone with a different perspective to help us recognize our strengths.

In a recent development, if you haven’t figured out your superpower yet, find people who will help you see it. And while you’re at it, be that person for someone else.

Listen to Kelly Cooper’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Do the Quiet Thing.”.

After six episodes of The Design Drop, I definitely don’t have all the answers—but I have more questions, latest perspectives, and some pretty great advice to carry with me.

What surprised me most was how different everyone’s path looked, yet how much of the same challenges kept coming up. That’s what I hope this podcast can be: a place to talk about the stuff we’re all trying to figure out, with people who’ve been there (and often still are).

Sources indicate that thanks to our first six guests for being so open, and to everyone who’s listened along. Here’s to more conversations, unexpected lessons, and figuring things out as we go.

Sources indicate that all six episodes of The Design Drop are available on SURROUND and wherever you listen to podcasts. This season of The Design Drop is presented by Haworth.

Caroline Murphy believes the future of design depends on how well the industry supports its next generation. As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, she develops community initiatives, programming, and recognition opportunities for Gen Z and early-career designers across brands including Interior Design, Metropolis, and LUXE Interiors + Design. A trained interior designer and graduate of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Murphy founded the Young Designers Collective in Nashville to help emerging designers learn, connect, and grow. Today, she's a speaker, connector, and self-described "Design Substantial Sister" dedicated to helping the emerging creatives find their place in the industry.

Industry News: Designing With Uncertainty: How AI Supercharges Probabilistic Thinking

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2024, an Air Canada customer asked a chatbot about bereavement fares. The bot confidently gave him a refund policy that didn’t exist. The airline refused to honor it. A tribunal ruled in the customer’s favor. The bot hadn’t decided anything; it had predicted an answer based on patterns in its training data. The company treated that prediction as policy.

Sources indicate that this is the risk at the heart of designing with AI today: probabilistic systems wrapped in deterministic interfaces. The AI offers a guess, the interface presents it as truth, and the user, or the organization, acts on it.

Humans are wired for deterministic thinking. We prefer to believe that past actions determine future outcomes. Flip a coin 999 times and get heads every time, the deterministic mind assumes the coin is rigged. The probabilistic mind accepts that the 1000th flip could still go either way. That second mindset is harder to hold onto, but it is exactly what designers need right now.

Products operate in complex, nonlinear environments, and AI is accelerating that complexity. When designers and product teams treat AI outputs as the answer rather than one of many possible answers, they build fragile experiences, and in some cases, like medical diagnostics or financial forecasting, genuinely dangerous ones.

According to recent reports, this article is a practical guide to designing probabilistically with AI as a partner. It is about using AI to sharpen your thinking rather than outsource it, accounting for model bias, human sentiment, and perceived risk along the way.

Most questions we ask AI do not produce binary answers. They produce probabilities based on patterns in data. If you ask, “Do aliens exist?” the answer will be somewhere between plausible and uncertain. Scientists consider life elsewhere in the universe likely, but without any concrete evidence, we cannot confirm it. The answer doesn’t resolve the question; it frames it as a probability.

Industry observers note that designers should read AI outputs the same way. They are signals, not conclusions, possible outcomes that have to be interpreted within the context of product goals, user behavior, and business constraints.

Industry observers note that many digital products already work this way. Netflix doesn’t know you’ll enjoy Superstore because you watched The Office; it estimates the probability and surfaces the title accordingly. The interface is responding to a prediction.

According to recent reports, design decisions can follow the same logic. AI models can combine behavioral analytics with research insights to estimate the likelihood of certain outcomes, and those probabilities can act as a yardstick for design strategy. Consider a scenario where analytics suggest a 60% versus 90% confidence that consumers will complete a purchase. At 60%, the design has to do more persuasive work, testimonials, explanations, comparisons, and reassurance signals may help the user move toward a decision. At 90%, the user is already motivated, and the design should start removing friction so the action can happen quickly. Same screen, very different design problem.

AI can also simulate outcomes using historical data and behavioral models before you commit to a direction. The value of those simulations depends heavily on how prompts are structured, the context they define, the hypothesis being tested, user motivation, and the edge cases you want stressed.

Industry observers note that I can think of one such practical use: evaluating early designs through structured prompts, especially when you don’t have direct access to the user group you’re designing for. The prompt below is a starting point for evaluating a design from the perspective of neurodivergent people as well. Treat it as a template, adapt the user group, criteria, and output format to your product, and use it as a conversation starter with your team rather than a verdict.

Recent findings suggest that that stated, simulations do not replace experimentation. Because models are trained on historical data, they reflect past behavior more strongly than they predict future change. Imagine designing a voice interface for elderly consumers who struggle with touchscreens. A model trained on mobile interaction data might predict low engagement, not because the idea lacks value, but because the dataset reflects different user behavior. Simulations should always surface assumptions, not prevent innovation.

Recent findings suggest that AI systems are built on historical data, more specifically, on the datasets they are trained on. That foundation shapes the outputs we receive. During the AI Summit in France, India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi shared an example that illustrates this well. If you ask an AI model to generate an image of a person writing with the left hand, the output may still show a person writing with their right hand. The reason is statistical: most people are right-handed, and the training data reflects that. This may have improved over time, but the point remains relevant. I still occasionally see this behavior when generating images with similar models.

What you receive is not truth. It is the most statistically likely outcome given the data available. Always ask whether past data meaningfully predicts future behavior. If additional context can improve the prediction, include it. Without context, the output is just one of many possible answers dressed up as the only one.

Industry observers note that confidence scores deserve the same scrutiny. Overtrusting a high-confidence output leads to the Air Canada situation. Dismissing a low-confidence one can cause teams to miss a real signal buried in noisy data. A prediction with 90% confidence is not necessarily correct, and a 40% signal is not necessarily useless. Designers must still weigh the possibilities, consider the case in front of them, and bring judgment to what the AI recommends.

Recent findings suggest that transparency is how you make that possible. As AI systems increasingly shape decisions, people need visibility into how outputs are generated, the sources, the reasoning, and the summaries behind a recommendation. Black-box systems breed distrust. Systems that reveal their reasoning let customers evaluate outputs for themselves. That transparency is good design and ethical practice. It respects the trust people place in these tools.

In a recent development, thinking in probabilities often means resisting the temptation of quick answers. AI can accelerate research and surface patterns faster than ever before, but those outputs are starting points, not final decisions.

According to recent reports, design shapes how a product is ultimately experienced — the decisions designers make determine whether the experience feels adequate, intuitive, or exceptional. And design is inherently full of assumptions and bets. Even the most rigorous research can yield multiple valid solutions to the same problem, each carrying a different probability of success.

Thinking probabilistically means recognizing that design decisions rarely produce binary outcomes. They lead to a range of possible results, and the role of the designer is to navigate those possibilities and identify the path most likely to create value. This mindset also builds adaptability: user needs evolve, strategies change, and sometimes ideas fail. Teams that lean on data signals, experimentation, and learning loops move faster toward the most effective solution.

Before the practical principles, one fundamental idea:.

Design decisions should be optimized for likelihood, not certainty.

Every design decision is a bet, not a guarantee. Even when decisions are informed by research and data, they are still based on smaller samples and assumptions about how users will behave at scale. A well-researched idea can still fail in the real world.

The Air Canada chatbot from the introduction is a design lesson as much as a legal one. The bot was doing what language models do, predicting plausible text. The interface, however, communicated that prediction with complete confidence, no caveats, no “here’s what our policy usually states,” no obvious path to a human. The user read confidence as commitment, and legally, so did the tribunal.

This is what happens when probabilistic systems are wrapped in deterministic interfaces. The interface transforms likelihood into certainty, and that is where the risk emerges.

Industry observers note that designers should avoid binary thinking — a great idea does not mean guaranteed success, and a familiar idea is not guaranteed to fail. Examine variations, confidence levels, and edge cases instead. AI can certainly help here, acting as a portfolio-thinking engine that surfaces different interpretations, highlights risks, and generates structured recommendations. The goal is not to optimize for certainty, but for value: it should always be value-driven.

Think of the moment in Avengers: Infinity War when Doctor Strange tells Tony Stark that out of millions of possible futures, there is only one where they win. AI cannot tell you the future, but it can help you explore the possible paths. Instead of asking whether an idea will succeed, ask AI to estimate the likelihood and get a score, and use those signals to guide decisions.

Recent findings suggest that even an actual probability is not a final answer. Imagine an AI model predicts an 80% likelihood that customers prefer a minimal checkout experience. That does not mean the solution is simply “build a minimal checkout.” Data should function as a compass, not a map.

These questions help designers validate predictions through usability testing and additional research. AI excels at identifying patterns, but it rarely explains why those patterns exist. Understanding motivation is still a human-centered research task.

The clearest cautionary tale here is Amazon’s experimental AI recruitment tool, which the manufacturer reportedly scrapped after discovering that the model had learned to downgrade resumes from women. The training data, roughly a decade of historical hiring decisions, was skewed toward male candidates, and the model inherited that skew. It began penalizing resumes that included the word “women’s,” as in “women’s chess club captain,” and favoring language more commonly found on men’s resumes. The system was not intentionally biased — the data was. Amazon reportedly tried to adjust it and eventually shut the project down because they could not guarantee it would not surface other discriminatory patterns.

Recent findings suggest that examples like this are why interpreting AI output critically matters. Designers need to understand the data behind a prediction and evaluate the reliability of the models they depend on. A recommendation is only as good as the data it was trained on, and the only way to know what that data is hiding is to ask.

Industry observers note that experimentation is usually framed as a way to validate a design decision. Want to lift the click-through rate of a CTA? Run an A/B test. Probabilistic thinking reframes this. Experiments should not only confirm solutions but also reduce uncertainty.

Traditional A/B testing is expensive. It costs engineering time, traffic allocation, and user exposure, especially when a losing variant runs against a significant chunk of your audience. AI simulations can help filter weaker ideas before they reach production by making experimentation more efficient. User needs shift constantly, and the most effective teams iterate fast.

AI can help evaluate assumptions early by modeling potential outcomes based on historical and behavioral data. These simulations act as a hypothesis filter, pointing to the directions worth investing engineering effort in. This also supports personalization — different customers may respond better to different experiences. Version A may resonate with high-intent users while version B works better for exploratory ones. Multiple experiences living side by side are not a flaw; they can be an intentional strategy.

It has been revealed that AI amplifies probabilistic thinking by surfacing scenarios, assigning likelihood scores, and enabling personalization at scale. Experimentation becomes a continuous feedback loop:.

Predict → Test → Learn → Adjust → Repeat!

Use this template to define the hypothesis:.

Industry observers note that we believe [behavioral assumption] will impact [metric] because [reason]. We’ll know we are right when [evidence].

Example: We believe simplifying the onboarding flow from 5 steps to 3 will increase completion rate because consumers experience decision fatigue when too many choices are presented. We’ll know we’re right when we see at least a 15% increase in step-to-step conversion with no drop in activation rate.

Sources indicate that one of the hardest things for designers is making uncertainty understandable and actionable. When uncertainty is hidden, users treat AI outputs as facts. When it’s communicated clearly, trust increases.

In a recent development, ranges, estimates, and confidence indicators go a long way. A delivery window of “Friday to Monday” tells the truth about variability without misleading anyone, whereas a specific timestamp that slips erodes trust every time. A face recognition feature that states “this looks like Pratik, is that right?” sets more honest expectations than one that just labels the photo with a name.

Communicating uncertainty does not weaken trust — it strengthens it. The goal is not to eliminate uncertainty but to design for it intelligently.

Different consumers respond to uncertainty differently, and your design should account for that:.

Recent findings suggest that AI should augment human judgment, and certainly not replace it. The most trustworthy systems are designed with clear moments where people can review, challenge, correct, or override machine suggestions. Human-in-the-loop (HITL) is not a safety net — it is a refinement engine. Every override, correction, or rejection becomes high-quality feedback that improves the model over time.

Industry observers note that control is a prerequisite for adoption. Consumers are more willing to rely on AI when they understand how a suggestion was generated, can evaluate its implications, and can easily intervene. Well-designed products make this explicit: who is acting, what happens if the suggestion is wrong, and where the user can step in.

Industry observers note that these interactions are also critical for system improvement. Every accept, reject, or edit is a strong signal, and compared to passive analytics, this kind of feedback produces far more meaningful training data. It closes the loop between real-world usage and model performance.

GitHub Copilot is a good everyday example. It offers inline code suggestions that developers can accept with a tab, edit, or ignore entirely. The system never commits code on the user’s behalf. Authorship stays with the humans. Every data point becomes implicit feedback about which suggestions were useful. Gmail’s Smart Compose works similarly, presenting predicted text as optional, keeping tone and intent in the user’s hands.

In higher-stakes contexts, HITL becomes more explicit. Risk and fraud systems typically use probability scores to route decisions: low-risk: proceed automatically; medium-risk: trigger additional verification; and high-risk: escalate to a human reviewer. This balances speed with judgment without removing oversight.

Industry observers note that in safety-critical domains like healthcare, human oversight is non-negotiable. AI may flag anomalies or suggest a diagnosis, but the clinician retains final authority. Tools that explain the details help the practitioner understand why a recommendation was made, reinforcing confidence without removing accountability.

From a UX perspective, HITL is about matching the interaction pattern to the level of risk. Simple accept/reject affordances work well for low-risk suggestions that improve speed without real consequences. As the stakes climb, impacting data, money, or people, preview and approval steps become essential. Explanations help users calibrate trust rather than blindly accept outputs.

Industry observers note that what happens behind the scenes matters just as much. The system should capture user decisions with context, feed them into learning workflows, and log overrides for auditability. Over time, teams can track signals like override rate, confidence accuracy, time-to-approval, and perceived trust. A high override rate is not a user failure. It is a signal that the design or the model needs attention.

Poorly implemented HITL systems can fail in subtle ways. Human review can devolve into a rubber stamp. Workflows can slow down so much that users route around the safeguards. Feedback can skew toward a narrow subset of users. These risks are real, but they are design problems, not reasons to remove HITL.

It has been revealed that the goal is not to maximize human involvement. It is to focus it where uncertainty, impact, or ethics demand it. Keeping HITL is less about control and more about clarity: clarity about who decides, when uncertainty matters, and how responsibility is shared between people and machines.

Recent findings suggest that good design adapts as the landscape shifts. Product design, especially in AI-powered systems, can no longer afford to optimize only for short-term conversion metrics. User intent is fluid as well as ever-changing, environments change rapidly, and probabilistic systems continuously evolve too. What works today can quietly break tomorrow. Designing for resilience means building products that stay reliable, trustworthy, and useful even as assumptions, data, and user behaviors change.

Resilient design shifts the question from:.

It has been revealed that how do we maximize this metric right now?! → How does this system behave over time, under stress, and in uncertainty?

A resilient system is one that:.

Do not just consider last quarter’s numbers. Peek into the following quarters to identify the shift and make changes accordingly.

It has been revealed that likelihoods shift constantly, AI models drift, contexts evolve, and user needs mature as well, so designing as if conditions are stable creates fragility in probabilistic environments. A resilient approach assumes volatility as the default.

In a recent development, think about how recommendation systems tend to evolve. The early version of a content feed optimizes for engagement, and for a while, engagement goes up. Then consumers start to notice the feed feels narrow, repetitive, maybe even exhausting. Resilient systems rebalance, introducing novelty, diversifying signals, and pulling in long-term satisfaction measures alongside short-term clicks.

Short-term conversion gains often hide long-term costs. Speeding up onboarding can reduce comprehension. Maximizing notification CTR can erode trust. Optimizing engagement alone can produce unhealthy usage patterns. Fragile systems maximize numbers while ignoring second-order effects, the downstream consequences that show up weeks or months later.

Recent findings suggest that duolingo’s hearts system is a good example of designing against this. It introduces friction: if you make too many mistakes, you run out of hearts and have to wait or practice older material to earn more. On paper, that looks like a conversion killer: fewer lessons per session. In practice, the team has publicly discussed how it supports long-term motivation and retention, which is the metric that actually matters for a learning app. Short-term engagement dips, but long-term outcomes improve.

According to recent reports, meta has made a similar, if more reluctant, shift. The tech giant publicly acknowledged that optimizing purely for “time spent” produced unintended emotional and societal effects, which led to a stated pivot toward “meaningful social interactions” as a guiding metric. Whether that shift fully landed is up for debate, but the acknowledgment itself is the point: optimizing for the wrong thing at scale has real downstream cost.

So, designers must routinely ask:.

Industry observers note that teams routinely plan for traffic spikes, but rarely for uncertainty spikes. Yet AI systems degrade, adversarial behaviors evolve, and external shocks can reshape user behavior overnight. Resilient design assumes variability and prepares for it.

Recent findings suggest that this means designing for degrading confidence. What does your interface do when the AI isn’t sure? Does it quietly fail, or does it gracefully hand off? Does the experience still make sense if AI assistance goes away entirely? A good fallback strategy is as important as the happy path.

If you take one thing from this article into your next design review, make it this:.

That single reframe changes how you write hypotheses, interpret AI output, scope experiments, and design for the moments when the system is wrong. Starting this week, name the assumption behind every AI recommendation you accept, find one place in your product where a probabilistic output is presented as a certainty, fix the framing, and design the fallback before the happy path.

The shift from deterministic to probabilistic design is less about new tools and more about a new posture. AI has not introduced uncertainty into our world. It has simply made the uncertainty that was always there impossible to ignore. AI can estimate, simulate, and recommend, but it cannot decide what matters, which owners are being overlooked, or which unconventional idea is worth defending against a model trained on yesterday’s data. Those remain human responsibilities. Think in ranges, not points. Test assumptions, not features. Build for adaptation, not perfection. In a world where prediction is cheap, and judgment is rare, the most valuable thing a designer can do is keep asking, What else might be true?

A Brooklyn Exhibition Rethinks the Art of the Candleholder

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A candleholder has a relatively simple job: keep a candle upright.
  • Geometric metalwork, organic silhouettes, and carved wood offer contrasting interpretations of the traditional candelabra.
  • It has been revealed that titled Candelabra Palaver, the exhibition opened Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A candleholder has a relatively simple job: keep a candle upright. Beyond that, the possibilities are nearly endless. At Piscina, a contemporary collectible design gallery in Brooklyn’s Red Hook neighborhood, approximately 80 artists and designers have taken that freedom to heart, creating their own interpretations of the everyday object for a new group exhibition.

Geometric metalwork, organic silhouettes, and carved wood offer contrasting interpretations of the traditional candelabra. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

It has been revealed that titled Candelabra Palaver, the exhibition opened Nov. 14, bringing together works selected through an open call. The brief was deliberately straightforward: make an object that holds a candle. With no prescribed materials, proportions, or aesthetic direction, participants could approach the assignment through their individual practices.

In a recent development, an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

The results explore just how much variation can emerge from a single functional requirement. Some contributors adhere to the familiar conventions of the candelabrum, while others push the object toward sculpture. Across the exhibition, differences in material, scale, and form reveal the many ways designers can interpret an object whose purpose has remained largely unchanged for centuries.

From a sculptural glass candelabra to a beaded floor-standing candleholder, the exhibition explores the relationship between materiality, scale, and function. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

The exhibition’s title hints at its playful premise: Palaver refers to idle talk, conversation, or unnecessary fuss, an apt description for a gathering of creative voices offering different opinions on something as seemingly uncomplicated as a candleholder.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Sources indicate that participating studios include Fort Standard, Kin & Company, Office of Tangible Spaces, Studio Daae, and Atelier Musset. Individual contributors include Sophie Collé, Steven Bukowski, Kaye Blegvad, Hanna Anonen, and Fitzhugh Karol, bringing together practitioners working across furniture, objects, art, and other creative disciplines.

Industrial forms mingle with playful figurative designs, including a carved wooden dog and a sculptural arrangement of flowers. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

In a recent development, the exhibition also reflects Piscina’s broader interest in the intersection of art, design, and craft. Founded in 2013 by artist and furniture designer Natalie Shook as a cooperative studio, Piscina has since evolved into a gallery and showroom dedicated to contemporary collectible design. Earlier this year, it introduced a dedicated gallery space alongside a reimagined showroom, expanding its platform for independent artists and designers.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Timed to coincide with the season of gatherings and candlelit evenings, Candelabra Palaver offers a reminder that even the most familiar household objects can provide fertile ground for experimentation. Whether restrained or exuberant, functional or sculptural, each piece begins with the same basic premise and arrives somewhere different.

Candelabra Palaver is on view until Dec. 31, 2026, at Piscina in Brooklyn, Upcoming York. All works in the exhibition are available for purchase.

In a recent development, lit candles cast warm pools of light and shadows across the surrounding surfaces, bringing another dimension to the sculptural objects. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

Industry News: The Best Coffee Table Books for Design Enthusiasts
