From Kickoff To First Concept: How To Turn Brand Strategy Into Visual Direction

📅 2026-07-10 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that anastasia Sycheva is the founder and art director of Feely Studio, a branding agency for technology startups.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • It has been revealed that when a branding project fails, it usually happens long before the logo stage: in the strategy phase, when words like “modern,” “trustworthy,” “premium,” “friendly,” and “disruptive” are left undefined.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that anastasia Sycheva is the founder and art director of Feely Studio, a branding agency for technology startups. Since 2016, she has helped SaaS, fintech, … More about Anastasia ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that when a branding project fails, it usually happens long before the logo stage: in the strategy phase, when words like “modern,” “trustworthy,” “premium,” “friendly,” and “disruptive” are left undefined. The result is a gap between what the brand is supposed to communicate and what the designer is expected to create. This is the space I like to call the “pre-concept” phase.

According to recent reports, at the beginning of a project, designers usually receive many inputs: a brief, a few stakeholder conversations, competitor references, maybe a moodboard or a list of adjectives. From there, they are expected to create visual concepts that feel right. But “right” is difficult to judge when the team has not agreed on what the brand is supposed to communicate in the first place.

As an example, a health tech organization we worked with said they wanted to look modern, trustworthy, and disruptive. At first, “disruptive” sounded like a push toward something bold and unconventional. But as we talked, it became clear that disruption, for them, still had to feel credible inside a conservative healthcare environment. Their clients were large government medical institutions. A brand that felt too rebellious, experimental, or visually loud would not create the right kind of trust.

In other words, their version of “disruptive” looked more traditional than the word suggested.

Industry observers note that the problem was not that the client used the wrong language. The problem was that the language was too broad to guide design decisions. Before a designer can turn strategy into a visual concept, those words need to become more specific. What kind of modern? Trustworthy in what way? Disruptive compared to whom? And how far can the brand move away from category expectations before it starts to feel wrong for its audience?

This article is about that pre-concept phase: the work that happens after the kickoff but before the first visual direction. While the broader brand identity process for digital products includes strategy, concepts, implementation, and the assets a product team needs to build consistently, this article focuses on the earlier work that makes the first concept possible: researching the brand context, uncovering hidden assumptions with stakeholders, and turning shared direction into a visual foundation. Rather, a practical bridge between what the brand needs to mean and how it might begin to look.

The first place to build that bridge is the brand workshop, where broad discovery needs to become a clearer understanding of the brand context.

A brand workshop will naturally cover the standard discovery topics: the business, its goals, the product or service, the competitive landscape, and the target audience. This article will not try to list every question a designer should ask in that workshop. For readers who want a broader starting point, we prepared a Brand Workshop Toolkit: Questions and Exercises, a FigJam framework we use in our studio to structure discovery conversations.

Recent findings suggest that here, I want to focus on a smaller set of questions that are easy to skip but extremely useful before visual work begins. These questions are less about collecting facts and more about clarifying perception. They help the team understand what the brand needs to make people believe, where it needs to feel credible, and which category assumptions it should follow or challenge.

Perception sits at the center of brand discovery because the brand is shaped in someone else’s mind.

If the brand ultimately lives in someone else’s perception, the workshop has to clarify what perception the team is trying to create.

The perception questions I focus on are:.

It has been revealed that these questions help reveal the assumptions behind people’s opinions, instead of simply adding more opinions to the room. The questions matter because brand attributes often sound aligned before they are actually understood. A stakeholder may say the brand should feel “premium,” and everyone may nod. But one person may mean refined and editorial. Another may mean expensive and exclusive. Another may mean clean, quiet, and minimal. The word sounds shared, but it can lead to three completely different visual systems.

It has been revealed that for instance, in the health tech project mentioned earlier, the client described the desired brand as “disruptive.” In many categories, that might suggest something bold, loud, or unconventional. But their audience was large government medical institutions, so disruption had to be expressed through clarity, efficiency, and confidence rather than rebellion. If we had taken the word at face value, the visual direction could easily have moved too far from what their audience would trust.

Industry observers note that in another project, a fintech team wanted the brand to feel “bold” without losing credibility. That word created useful tension. The word bold could mean bright colors, oversized typography, and a highly expressive system. But in a financial category, it also had to carry signals of security, control, and competence. The question was not whether the brand should be bold, but what kind of boldness would still feel trustworthy.

Sources indicate that when the team can define what these attributes mean in context, the designer is no longer working from broad adjectives. They are working from a clearer design problem.

According to recent reports, strategically selected questions can uncover part of the verbal layer, but words alone are rarely enough. To move from language into visual direction, it helps to incorporate exercises that make stakeholders think through images, associations, and relative perception.

Jake Knapp makes a similar point in GV’s Three-Hour Brand Sprint:.

The following two exercises help translate what stakeholders say about the brand into material that can later inform look and feel, design principles, and concept development.

It has been revealed that this is also where stakeholder participation becomes key. When clients only receive a strategy presentation, they can stay passive. They may agree in the meeting without noticing the assumptions they are bringing into the process. But when they have to place a competitor on a map, choose an image, or explain why a certain reference feels credible, they become active participants. Their attitudes, beliefs, and disagreements become visible before they have a chance to derail the first concept review.

I usually start by looking outward at the category, then inward at the brand itself.

According to recent reports, before the workshop, collect screenshots of competitor brands, websites, product interfaces, social visuals, or other visible brand touchpoints. During the workshop, ask the client team to place those competitors on a simple two-axis map.

In a recent development, this exercise is not about deciding which competitors have “good” or “bad” design. It is about understanding how the client reads the category: what feels credible, what feels generic, what feels too conservative, what feels too experimental, and where there may be an open visual territory for the brand.

Recent findings suggest that the axes should be chosen based on the tension the brand needs to solve. For example:.

Industry observers note that for a health tech firm that wants to feel innovative but works with conservative medical institutions, the map might use traditional to progressive and corporate to human. For a fintech brand that wants to stand out without losing trust, it might use understated to bold and accessible to exclusive.

The most useful part of this exercise is often not the final map, but the disagreement it creates. One stakeholder may read a competitor as progressive, while another sees it as generic. One may see a brand as premium, while another reads it as cold. These disagreements reveal how different people define trust, innovation, credibility, and differentiation. That is exactly the kind of ambiguity that needs to be resolved before design begins.

Industry observers note that after the team has discussed the category, I like to turn the conversation inward. One exercise we use for this is called Visual Brand Driver. Each stakeholder is asked to choose images for a set of unrelated categories: transport, typeface, activity, furniture, mood, object, animal, architecture, and drink.

Recent findings suggest that the instruction is crucial: the images should not represent the person’s personal taste. They should represent the firm.

In a recent development, for example, if the company were a type of transport, what would it be? A quiet electric car, a high-speed train, a private jet, a bicycle, a delivery van? If it were a piece of furniture, would it be a soft lounge chair, a precise modular desk, or a heavy boardroom table?

Industry observers note that after choosing the images, each person adds four or five adjectives to explain why they selected them. This part matters more than the image itself. The same object can mean different things to different people. A train might suggest speed, structure, reliability, mass accessibility, or a fixed route. A lounge chair might suggest comfort, calm, informality, or lack of urgency.

The exercise helps create a deeper layer of brand perception. Instead of asking people to describe the company directly, it asks them to think through metaphor and association. Patterns and contradictions become visible. One stakeholder may see the brand as refined and calm, another as energetic and experimental. One may describe the company as precise and structured, another as warm and flexible.

Recent findings suggest that those differences are not a problem. They are useful materials. They show what needs to be clarified before the visual concept phase begins.

According to recent reports, this exercise is also helpful because it separates brand perception from aesthetic preference. A stakeholder may personally like a certain image, but if it does not describe the company, it should not be part of the exercise. That distinction is important throughout the branding process. The question is not “Do we like this?” but “Does this express the right thing about the brand?”.

It has been revealed that once the workshop has revealed the main assumptions, the next client meeting can turn that shared understanding into a visual foundation. This is still not the first identity concept. It is a working layer between strategy and design, where the client can react to perception, visual principles, and early asset directions before the designer invests time in full concepts.

We usually structure this meeting around three connected layers:.

Together, these layers move the conversation from perception to practical design boundaries.

Look and feel boards are not collections of visuals the team likes. They are perception boards. The designer collects references based on the workshop: desired perception, category tension, competitor codes, stakeholder disagreements, and brand character.

If the brand needs to feel trustworthy, modern, and human, the board should help the team discuss what kind of trust, modernity, and humanity are appropriate. Is the brand calm and institutional, or warm and accessible? Is it progressive through precision, or through a more expressive editorial tone?

The point is to let the client respond to perception before reacting to a logo, color palette, or finished visual system.

Design code makes the direction more specific by translating key brand ideas into visual principles.

Sources indicate that for a parenting app in Germany, personalized support for your unique journey might become organic shapes, handwritten lines, and softer compositions. Parenting is messy and magical might become soft gradients, layered imagery, and playful irregularity. Research-backed support for real life might introduce doctor calls, data snapshots, infographics, and editorial layouts that make the brand feel credible.

In a recent development, for a PR agency working with prop tech companies, momentum in motion might become lines, arrows, ripple effects, or motion blur. Springboard might become a lift-off moment and elastic visual energy. Building blocks might become modular shapes or stacked compositions.

It has been revealed that the team is not choosing the final graphic expression here. It is testing whether the visual metaphors make sense before concept design begins.

The final layer brings the conversation down to the building blocks of identity: typography, color, logo style, photography, illustration, and graphic language.

At this stage, the team can discuss questions such as:.

Recent findings suggest that this gives the designer boundaries without making the final identity predictable. The next step is still concept design, but the team is no longer starting from vague adjectives or private expectations.

According to recent reports, before moving into the first concept, it helps to pause and check whether the team has enough shared direction. The checklist is not meant to make every decision in advance. It is meant to make sure the designer is not starting from vague words, hidden assumptions, or unresolved disagreements.

Before creating the first concept, check whether the team has:.

Industry observers note that this last point is especially useful. A strong pre-concept phase not only tells the designer what to explore. It also clarifies what to avoid: directions that would be too expected, too cold, too playful, too conservative, too loud, too generic, or too far from what the audience can trust.

When the team can name those boundaries, the first concept becomes easier to evaluate. The conversation shifts from “I like it” or “I do not like it” to “Does this express the brand we agreed on?”.

Industry observers note that the first concept should not feel like a guess or a surprise reveal. It should feel like the next step in a direction the team already understands.

That does not mean removing intuition, experimentation, or creative risk from the branding process. It means giving those things a sharper problem to solve. When the team has clarified the brand character, tested visual perception, translated ideas into design principles, and discussed the early building blocks of the identity, the designer can explore with more confidence.

Pre-concept work does not need to make the final identity predictable. It needs to make the conversation around it more meaningful. Instead of asking whether the work matches someone’s private expectation, the team can ask a better question: Does this visual direction express what the brand needs to become?

#115386. Latest Update: Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1444 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that india’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November.
  • Sources indicate that the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for big works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses.
  • For India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that india’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November. While several Indian dealers said that a date clash with Diwali had resulted in quieter VIP days than last year, this amounted to most local exhibitors selling around half, rather than all their stands.

Sources indicate that the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for big works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses. The country’s secondary art market recorded its best year ever in 2025, at $272.1m, according to a recent report by the wealth managers 360One (a sponsor of the fair).

For India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion. “This fair is great for us, and right now I feel more inclined to invest my effort here than fairs abroad,” stated Hena Kapadia, the founder of the dynamic local gallery Tarq, which sold the majority of its stand—including photographs by the Kolkata-based filmmaker Ronny Sen referencing post-humanism—and rehung around 50% of it.

According to recent reports, notable sales in the fair’s contemporary section included a Subodh Gupta painting at the Delhi- and Mumbai-based Nature Morte, which placed to a fresh buyer of Indian-origin based in Europe, for €350,000. The gallery’s director Roma Patel noted that she met new collectors from south India, and diaspora collectors from Los Angeles, as well as existing clients, at the fair.

In the Modern tent, “some punchy prices” were noted by one auction executive. Works acquired at auction within the past 12 months were flipped for tidy profits, including M F Husain's 1991 Untitled (Horses & Ganesh) at Akar Prakar, bought from Bonhams in December 2025 for £179,000 (equivalent to $234,000) and resold for $600,000, although likely with a hefty discount.

Subtler gestures of confidence were also observed. Grosvenor Gallery, which counted among its sales a painting by the Sri Lankan Senaka Senanayake for a shade over $100,000, decided not to send out PDFs to its clients prior to the fair. "We haven’t pre-sold anything for the past few fairs—a nice luxury afforded to us by the current market conditions, though it won’t last forever,” mentioned the gallery’s director Charlie Moore.

Art Mumbai takes place at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse.

Industry observers note that with India’s place on the global stage growing, and the predominant art markets of the US, Europe and China remaining relatively muted, international players are circling. Case in point, Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox, and Art Basel’s director of fairs Vincenzo de Bellis and head of VIP Carly Murphy, all attended Art Mumbai for the first time this year. Fox remarked this was his first India trip for work. Meanwhile, Art Basel’s India VIP representative Shaan Shahani noted that this visit marked the first India trip by Art Basel top brass in a decade.

According to recent reports, also testing these waters are the 12 international galleries that indicated at Art Mumbai this year, up from seven last year. Newcomers included the global dealership Perrotin, Richard Saltoun and Niru Ratnam from London, and Rizq from Abu Dhabi, while Lisson, Continua, Ben Brown and Gallery Isabelle all returned from last year. Three international galleries that took part last year did not come back: Rossi & Rossi (Hong Kong); Leila Heller (Newly introduced York and Dubai) and Saskia Fernando (Colombo).

Several of these large galleries continued to play it safe, bringing presentations to suit interior design-focused sensibilities and algorithmically informed taste—plenty of reflective surfaces, legible motifs and name brands, such as Ai Weiwei and Anish Kapoor. Lisson's sales topped out at £1.2m, and included two of Kapoor’s signature concave disc sculptures. On the closing day, gallery director Ellie Harrison-Read said that she had a "good fair, but closing a few more sales could make it great”.

It has been revealed that by and large, galleries that brought subtler or nicher works struggled. Niru Ratnam, which indicated small paintings in muted palettes by the late Bengali-British Modernist Amal Ghosh and the British Indian Bhajan Hunjan, did not place a work for the first two days, having pre-sold one painting by Ghosh to cover stand and shipping costs.

Sources indicate that while both Ghosh and Hunjan are increasingly being reappraised by world leading institutions such as Tate, they are relatively unknown figures in both the UK and India and have proved a tough sell in Mumbai. As one local dealer noted, "I rarely meet collectors here who lead with curiosity or instinct".

Sources indicate that another litmus test for this market was a painting by Robert Nava, brought by the first-time exhibitor Night gallery from Los Angeles. Nava, who is co-represented by Pace, is a US-based market star whose naive figurative style sharply divides critics. The secondary-market painting, depicting a swimming cat, was tagged at $220,000, a hefty price for a buying pool unfamiliar with his work and where contemporary art by the most established artists rarely exceeds $400,000. It did not sell by the fair’s last day, but the gallery’s director Davida Nemeroff remarked she had engaged in several serious enquiries, including one local buyer who went home to measure their wall following a conversation on the stand. “We went in pretty blind, and didn’t know what to expect”, she said.

Sources indicate that the gallery did however sell to the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art a $16,000 painting installation by Divya Mehra embossed with words from a speech by Surya Kant, India's chief justice, that sparked the Cockroach Janata Party protests. “We’ve learned that if you don’t bring something vaguely South Asian, or a Picasso, it won’t sell," Nemeroff mentioned.

Speaking of Picasso, a 1930s painting by the Spanish master was offered by Ben Brown, carrying a $4.5m price tag—the most expensive work brought to the fair in its four editions. Last year, the gallery revealed a smaller painting by Picasso to Art Mumbai, which did not sell. Rather than being discouraged, gallery director Hugo Cobb decided to double down. “Our feedback was that this market is now discerning enough for quality and it doesn’t want anything second rate,” he said.

According to recent reports, the gallery did not sell the Picasso by the end of the fair, with Cobb attesting to the fact that the very top end of the Indian market still amounts to a handful of collectors. "There are maybe four or five collectors in this country who would buy it, and none of them did." The gallery did, however, sell a monumentally scaled Yoan Capote painting, embedded with fishhooks, for $1m to a local collector. Cobb added that should the gallery return to Art Mumbai, it will focus on bringing high value secondary market material.

As many international visitors and exhibitors will have observed, India now has no shortage of deep pocketed buyers, but its tastes remain local and largely conservative. "Collecting in India is largely informed by familiarity," claims the adviser Yamini Mehta. "The market here is still not ready for super conceptual stuff.".

Further factors that keep India's art market more domestically focused than other Asian art hubs include stifling bureaucracy and high taxes involved in shipping works in and out of the country. As the Richard Saltoun director Sakshi Mahajan stated, "they don't make it easy or cheap to bring in art. Even when it's worth relatively small amounts".

Industry observers note that meanwhile, complications of black money circulating in the Indian art market persist. As one adviser, speaking anonymously, noted, "many Indians might not want to send money abroad, for fear of those transactions being registered by the RBI (Reserve Bank of India)".

India's art market growth indeed appears to be a domestic success story. This is in contrast to its last boom in the 2000s, which was fuelled by speculative buying, often from overseas collectors with no ties to the region.

While in buzzier Asian art markets like Seoul and Hong Kong, many collectors covet international—usually Western—names at the expense of local talent, India overwhelmingly supports its own artists: representatives from a growing number of new Indian biennials were spotted at the fair, including from the Bengal Biennial and the soon-to-launch Benares Biennial, both of whose artist lists are heavily weighted towards India and the wider South Asian region.

While India might not yet be ready for a truly international fair or an outpost of a mega gallery, it appears to be building something more valuable: an infrastructural network supporting homegrown talent, which should help to safeguard against another crash when the market eventually enters a soberer period.

#115385. No, People Don’t Want More AI In Their Life

📅 2026-07-15 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1210 w)

No, People Don’t Want More AI In Their Life

📅 2026-07-15 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1210 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Many companies silently assume that everybody wants more AI in their lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Many companies silently assume that everybody wants more AI in their lives. That people are craving newly introduced AI features, new AI products, new AI workflows — that would all magically replace all existing outdated practices and broken ways of working.

But in reality, it seems like people don’t want more AI at all — at least not in the way most AI leaders envision it. Unsurprisingly, many AI features have low adoption and retention — at a very high cost of delivery, and a high risk of reputation damage.

Recent findings suggest that it’s remarkably difficult to make a strong argument with senior leadership, but AI is not a value proposition. New AI features don’t magically make for happy or excited customers. Because AI features are often bolt-ons and separate tools for employees to use, they typically take people out of their regular way of working.

AI is pretty good at amplifying shortcuts and shortcomings in organizations — from data quality to decision making. It can’t magically fix years of accumulated quick patches, technical debt, broken culture and internal politics. If anything, they become more visible with AI as inconsistencies or conflicting priorities and get handed directly to owners, who are then left to make sense of the mess themselves.

In a recent development, because in most organizations, work typically requires hopping on and off between plenty of disconnected and fragmented systems, with a newly introduced AI tool, they now have yet another system that they also need to hop on and off. Often it produces more work, and typically it’s not particularly rewarding work either.

It has been revealed that on top of that, people are very much aware of the cost of finding and fixing AI hallucinations. Asking AI to generate a response might feel easier than writing from scratch, but it has a cost:.

For many people, AI isn’t something they can proactively choose and explore on their own — it arrives uninvited, at someone else’s pace. On top of that, plenty of messages amplify fears and worries about AI replacing work — so it’s hardly surprising that the perception of AI isn’t excitement. It’s resistance to change and deep anxiety about one’s place in a world that seems to be changing without them.

At best, AI features might be silently accepted or nodded away. At worst, AI raises concerns, doubts, caution — and calls for a healthy dose of skepticism. And sometimes it’s perceived as a threat or liability — because unlike other features, AI is neither predictable nor reliable.

People don’t dream of AI art museums or AI fridges or AI hotel reception or AI-narrated children’s books. They don’t want their children to have romantic AI partners. Most people don’t want to actively manage (and clean up after) a swarm of AI agents roaming in their bank accounts and acting on their behalf in the real world. And most notably, people don’t really want a magical box to speak to or type into all the time.

According to recent reports, I’m always puzzled by the comparison of AI features with how unreliable humans are. But people don’t compare software with other people. They compare features with features — and if one feature in one product is unreliable, while a similar feature works flawlessly in another, they choose the latter. It’s not about AI or not AI, but rather what works consistently and reliably, and what doesn’t.

Many conversations about AI are conversations about the speed of delivery. But to many people, there is little value in increasing the speed of delivery. They want to do things well, with enough time to think and make good decisions. They also want to enjoy the time they spend working on things, rather than just ship faster. There is an enormous feeling of reward and achievement that slowly disappears, one vibe-coded change at a time.

People don’t change much. And after all these years, they (still) want features that are fast, accessible, reliable, predictable and useful — every single time. And ideally not the ones that replace their entire workflow, but that augment their way of working — and that take over the most mundane, annoying, and boring tasks that they find no pleasure in.

In a recent development, many jobs are exposed to AI automation, but in many of them there is a rewarding, unique, creative part that requires taste, point of view, and perhaps even human intuition. And if AI automates boring parts of it, that’s an advantage for everyone. That’s also what enhances productivity and brings more joy in daily life.

When AI automates tedious and mentally exhausting tasks, its value is much easier to grasp. But for that, AI shouldn’t feel like a bolt-on. It should be deeply integrated into people’s existing workflows. It must also match existing mental models that they have developed and fine-tuned for years or decades. AI should adapt to how people think and make decisions, not the other way around.

In a recent development, and it doesn’t really matter if these features are branded as “AI”, “smart” or “automation”. However, they must work well for people using them. And that means that people must be aware of use cases where it actually helps them, and be inspired to find more use cases on their own.

It has been revealed that ironically, tools that work well there aren’t “AI-first” — they are “AI-second”. Subtle, humble, calm, ambient, taking a supportive role in the background for work that otherwise is remarkably dull and unnecessary.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps I’m missing a bigger picture, and perhaps I’m just old school — but I really do like people. Their stories, their thinking, their emotions, their enthusiasm, their laughing. AI can be remarkably helpful in many situations, but so are people. And between the two, I would favor spending time with a human — however imperfect they are — every single time.

No, people don’t need more AI in their lives — they need AI to automate all the boring stuff they have to deal with every day, so they have more time and headspace to do things that they actually love and enjoy doing. That doesn’t mean spending more time with AI — but spending more time with people they love.

#115384. Is Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) Worth It? The Hidden Costs

📅 23 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1239 w)

Is Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) Worth It? The Hidden Costs

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1239 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that what's your FI number?
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • Buy Now Pay Later services let you split a purchase into installments — typically four payments over six weeks (Afterpay, Klarna "Pay in 4") or monthly payments over 3-36 months (Affirm, Klarna financing).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Avg Spending Increase with BNPL.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Buy Now Pay Later services let you split a purchase into installments — typically four payments over six weeks (Afterpay, Klarna "Pay in 4") or monthly payments over 3-36 months (Affirm, Klarna financing). The checkout process is seamless: enter your name and email, get instantly approved, and walk away with your purchase having paid only the first installment.

It has been revealed that BNPL providers make money in two ways. First, they charge merchants 4-8% of each transaction — significantly more than the 2-3% credit card processing fee. Merchants accept this because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50%. Second, some providers charge interest on longer-term prepares, and nearly all charge late fees when you miss a payment.

The "interest-free" label on short-term prepares deserves scrutiny. While you may not pay interest, the behavioral cost is substantial. Research from multiple financial studies demonstrates that BNPL users spend 30-50% more per transaction than they would with cash or debit. The psychological separation of the purchase from the full payment removes the natural spending brake that keeps budgets in check.

In a recent development, the financial industry has known for decades that separating the moment of purchase from the moment of payment increases spending. Credit cards exploit this. BNPL takes it further by making the payment feel even smaller — "just four easy payments of $37.50" feels dramatically different from "$150" even though it is the same amount.

It has been revealed that A 2026 survey found that 43% of BNPL customers have missed at least one payment. Among those who missed payments, the average person missed three or more over the prior year. Late fees compound rapidly — four missed $8 Afterpay fees on a $200 purchase adds $32, effectively creating a 16% surcharge on what was supposed to be interest-free.

The credit score impact is evolving rapidly. As recently as 2022, most BNPL activity was invisible to credit bureaus. That has changed. Affirm now reports all payment activity to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna reports financing plans to all three bureaus. On-time BNPL payments may slightly help your score, but missed payments can drop it significantly — and the damage lasts up to seven years.

Recent findings suggest that for anyone pursuing financial independence, BNPL represents the opposite of the FI mindset. FI is built on intentional spending, high savings rates, and letting compound growth work in your favor. BNPL encourages impulsive spending, fragments your cash flow, and creates obligations that reduce your ability to invest.

There is exactly one scenario where BNPL is financially rational: a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you would have paid the full price regardless. For example, you need a fresh dishwasher, you have the $800 in savings, and the retailer offers four interest-free payments. You keep your $800 invested for six more weeks while paying in installments. The benefit is tiny — a few dollars of investment returns — but the cost is genuinely zero if you make every payment on time.

Outside this narrow scenario, BNPL is almost always a worse choice than the alternatives.

The financial independence community is nearly unanimous: BNPL is a trap disguised as convenience. The entire BNPL business model depends on you spending more than you planned. If you were going to buy the item anyway and you have the cash, just buy it. If you do not have the cash, that is your budget telling you something important.

Industry observers note that the question to ask before any BNPL checkout: "Would I buy this right now if I had to pay the full price in cash today?" If the answer is no, BNPL is not helping you afford something — it is helping you overspend. If the answer is yes, just pay cash and skip the installment tracking, the payment reminders, and the risk of a missed payment damaging your credit.

For those building toward financial independence, every dollar matters. The 30-50% spending increase that BNPL encourages directly reduces your savings rate — the single most crucial variable in determining how rapidly you reach FI.

The average ChooseFI listener saves $24,000+ with an expert student loan plan.

Trusted by Brad Barrett, Co-founder and Host, ChooseFI.

Sources indicate that mortgage lenders are increasingly scrutinizing BNPL obligations during the underwriting process. Multiple active BNPL aims — even if interest-free — show up as recurring liabilities and can affect your debt-to-income ratio. If you are planning to apply for a mortgage or auto loan in the next 6-12 months, pay off all BNPL balances and avoid opening new ones. Lenders view fragmented installment obligations as a sign of cash flow stress, even if you have never missed a payment.

Affirm is a legitimate, publicly traded company (AFRM on NASDAQ). It is safe in the sense that it will not steal your money or identity. However, being legitimate does not mean it is a good financial decision. Affirm's interest rates range from 0-36% APR depending on creditworthiness, and the company reports all payment activity to credit bureaus.

Increasingly, yes. Affirm reports to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna financing looks report to all three bureaus. On-time payments may help slightly, but a single missed payment can significantly damage your score and remains on your report for up to seven years.

It has been revealed that afterpay charges an $8 late fee per missed payment, capped at 25% of the order value. After multiple missed payments, your account is suspended, the balance is sent to collections, and the delinquency is reported to Equifax. Collections accounts damage your credit score severely and remain for seven years.

It has been revealed that klarna's "Pay in 4" plan is interest-free with no late fees, but your account may be suspended for missed payments. Klarna's longer-term financing plans charge 7.99-33.99% APR, involve a hard credit pull, and report to all three credit bureaus. Read the terms carefully — the word "Klarna" covers very different products.

It is possible but unlikely for most people. Research consistently shows that BNPL increases spending by 30-50% per transaction. If you have the discipline to use BNPL only on planned, budgeted purchases at 0% interest — and never miss a payment — the financial harm is minimal. But for most users, the behavioral cost exceeds any convenience benefit.

Because it works — for the store. Merchants pay BNPL providers 4-8% of each transaction (vs 2-3% for credit cards) because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50% and reduces cart abandonment by 20-30%. The merchant is paying for you to spend more. That should tell you who this arrangement benefits.

Buy Now Pay Later is a marketing innovation designed to make you spend more — and the data confirms it works. BNPL owners spend 30-50% more per transaction, 43% miss payments, and the credit reporting implications are growing. The only responsible use case is a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you already have the cash. For everyone else, especially those pursuing financial independence, BNPL is a detour in the wrong direction. Pay with cash, invest the difference, and let compound growth work for you instead of against you.

#115382. When It Makes Sense To “Block” The Main Thread

📅 2026-07-17 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2095 w)

When It Makes Sense To “Block” The Main Thread

📅 2026-07-17 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2095 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ok, but seriously, I’m a web and mobile developer who writes a lot.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Industry observers note that we’ve all heard of the sacred rule in modern web development, the rule never to be broken.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I Code. I Write. Meme Rules. Ok, but seriously, I’m a web and mobile developer who writes a lot. In my spare time, I like to build products that would … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that we’ve all heard of the sacred rule in modern web development, the rule never to be broken. The rule of “Never block the main thread.”.

Industry observers note that you almost can’t miss it as a web developer; it’s in almost every performance guide, and to be fair, it is good advice. We all know the browser’s main thread is single-threaded, meaning it can only do one thing at a time.

In a recent development, plus, as we know, the main thread isn’t ours alone; we share it with the browser’s rendering engine, input handlers, and other critical tasks. As a result, the less time we hold onto the main thread, the more responsive an app feels. That leads us to share tasks with background workers as we’ve convinced ourselves there should be a hard line between the UI and any computation, and that line shouldn’t be crossed.

And that is what a “recommended” architecture looks like.

But I dare say that *sometimes*, moving the data to a worker is slower than just letting the main thread do the work.

It has been revealed that I found this out a few months ago while building a Chrome extension with screenshotting features called Fastary. I kept finding a latency of about 2 to 3 seconds in all my testing, even after using an Offscreen Document (a background process in Chrome extensions) to handle the canvas operations. A screenshot task should feel instant without lag, after all.

It is quite ironic that by reflex, we move work away from the main thread to avoid freezing the UI, but sometimes the act of moving that work (e.g., serializing, copying, and deserializing) can also freeze the UI. And sometimes the recommended approach of letting the background do the work can be slower than just doing the work on the main thread.

To put things in perspective, let’s understand why we isolate browser contexts and how they communicate with each other, with emphasis on the communication part.

According to recent reports, A browser is more than a single environment. Different environments are running at the same time, each having its own memory space, what it can access, and rules:.

In a recent development, each one of these is isolated from the others. A web worker or background script lives in a different memory space from the main thread. They cannot just reach and read each other’s variables or logic, and this is known as the “shared-nothing” architecture.

How do these isolated environments communicate? They explicitly message each other back and forth using APIs, like postMessage().

postMessage() tells the browser to take a piece of data and deliver it to the context that requested it. But to do this, the browser relies on the Structured Clone Algorithm (SCA).

According to recent reports, you’re probably familiar with JSON.stringify(). SCA is similar, but much stronger and smarter. In its simplest form, SCA is a deep, recursive copy operation, i.e., cloning. It walks through the entire data structure it is given, clones every single value, serializes it into a transportable format, ships those bytes to the target contexts, and then reconstructs the original object on the receiving side.

Sources indicate that SCA is fast, or maybe fast-ish… For a small regular config object like {theme: "dark"}, it is imperceptible; you don’t even notice it. The story changes, however, when dealing with heavy data because the SCA is a synchronous blocking O(n) operation, i.e., the cost increases linearly with the size of your data.

Recent findings suggest that let’s put that into perspective. A user clicks a button, and internally, an 8MB image payload is sent to a background worker for processing. When you call postMessage(), the main thread must immediately stop what it is doing to run this serialization and copying process.

Sources indicate that I’m sure some of you are already thinking, “Why not just use Transferable objects?” And that is a valid point. Let’s talk about that.

It has been revealed that developers who really pursue ultra-high-performance web apps usually use Transferable objects (e.g., ArrayBuffer, ImageBitmap, or MessagePort) to bypass the Structured Clone Algorithm. This is because when you transfer an object, you’re not making a copy (like SCM). Instead, the browser switches ownership of the data from one context to another.

The browser performs a hand-off whereby the sending context loses access to the data instantly, and the receiving context takes full control. It is actually insanely fast. According to Chrome Developers’ benchmark, transferring a massive 32MB ArrayBuffer can take under 7ms, compared to about 300ms when cloning with SCM. That’s a 43x speed boost.

In a recent development, but like all good things, there are downsides. To name a few:.

So, as far as my screenshot extension went, Transferable objects were not an option.

It has been revealed that why do we even bother isolating contexts at all? Why not just leave it all to the main thread?

Recent findings suggest that offloading long-running CPU tasks to a background thread is absolutely the right thing to do. The browser needs to paint a newly introduced frame every 16.6ms to keep things fluid; that means any task that takes >50ms is generally considered “long”. Offloading to the background is absolutely the right thing to do.

The issue, however, is that we’ve turned this “never block the main thread” into an absolute rule, without asking is this task expensive to process or expensive to move?

I have come to realize now that the rule is less “never block the main thread” than “never block the main thread for too long.”.

My goal with the Fastary extension was to make it feel like a native app, running as smoothly and instantly as you would expect a native app to.

It has been revealed that as you already know, I took the recommended approach to use the Offscreen Document to handle DOM work in the background. But to my surprise, that took a different turn.

Sources indicate that the Offscreen Document API is a clear winner. You create a hidden, undisplayed document that runs entirely in the background. It has a DOM and supports Canvas. For example, if I want to crop a screenshot, stitch multiple screenshots together, perform heavy image manipulation, or add a watermark, Offscreen Document was made for that.

In a recent development, turns out that was not the best approach. This was my architecture:.

Industry observers note that but when I tested it, the screenshot didn’t feel instant. As I said earlier, there was a consistent 2–3 second lag.

According to recent reports, I figured out that when captureVisibleTab() takes a screenshot, it returns a Base64 URL string, and on a standard 1080p screen, that string could be approximately 1MB or more, depending on how detailed the image is. It gets even more interesting on modern Retina displays (e.g., MacBooks) as they tend to automatically double the image’s size by default.

Keep in mind that since the image payload could be doubled and extension messaging relies on JSON serialization (as of this writing), we potentially deal with massive synchronous communication that costs an entire round trip.

Recent findings suggest that the image string data is JSON-serialized at least twice: once when going into the Offscreen Document and once coming back out with the processed results to the background worker. The actual image processing (cropping) done inside the Offscreen Document was fast, no doubt, but I can’t say the same about the transfer overhead.

Sources indicate that as if the latency itself wasn’t enough, I noticed a rather subtle bug — which, now that I think of it, was more of my ignorance. After a screenshot was taken, the crop result was completely off in a way that either weirdly scaled the image or resulted in incorrect coordinates.

Recent findings suggest that it turns out that when a user selects a region to crop, the content script gets the box coordinates using getBoundingClientRect(), which is measured in CSS pixels; this is what the DOM uses. But when the screenshot is captured natively in Chrome, the browser doesn’t crop it automatically; it instead uses the physical hardware pixels to get the full screen capture. And the browser uses devicePixelRatio (DPR) to know how many physical pixels should represent one CSS pixel. Basically, if a user on a Retinal display (DPR = 2) highlights an area of 400x300 CSS pixels, the actual captured image area is 800x600 physical pixels.

According to recent reports, for an accurate crop, I needed to apply these two different measurement systems with the right DPR, i.e., scale the crop coordinates by the DPR. But remember, Offscreen Documents have no physical display. Processing any image would have a default DPR equal to 1. To fix this, I would have to capture the exact devicePixelRatio from the active tab, serialize it, pass it alongside the image payload, and manually do the scaling math inside the Offscreen Document. The complexity starts to compound.

What if I broke the golden rule and did the work on the main thread instead?

Some developers will argue that UI tasks are the only things that should run on the main thread, but I don’t fully agree with that. Personally, I believe that user explicitly-invoked actions that need immediate results can sometimes get a solid pass to run on the main thread, provided the work is incredibly fast (e.g., 1s).

Industry observers note that that’s what I did: scrap out the Offscreen Document and reengineer the logic. Instead of:.

…I decided to run the whole image processing in the active tab:.

According to recent reports, this approach completely clears out multiple context hops and round trips that JSON serialization requires. The only cross-context transfer involves sending the data URL from the background to the content script.

The Retina DPI concern essentially solved itself, as the content script runs directly inside the real, active browser tab because it knows the monitor’s real devicePixelRatio.

But there’s an elephant in the room that you may have noticed.

Sure, the image is now processed on the main thread, and the background manipulates the canvas in the active tab. I could technically be blocking the main thread. That’s where I amended the “no blocking the main thread” rule to “no blocking the main thread for too long.” In this specific case, at least, blocking the main thread for a task the user requests for approximately one second is justifiable. It works conversely as well: maybe don’t isolate processes if the data transfer cost is greater than the processing cost.

I’ve boiled it down to a mental model that depends on whether the task is:.

These are tasks where the primary cost is computation and not the size of the data itself. These are tasks where most of the time is spent on doing calculations or heavy transformations, e.g., image compression, audio profiling, physics simulation, etc.

The transfer cost for these tasks is minuscule compared to the actual work.

These tasks are the exact opposite. These tasks are only expensive because of the size. The processing time is almost insignificant, but the data is expensive to transport, e.g., image cropping, filtering an array, shallow copy, etc.

In a recent development, in my specific case, offloading the task to the background falls mostly into negative-sum efficiency. If we are talking about moving megabytes of data to perform a 50ms operation, there is no benefit to offloading it to the background.

Perhaps we can think of it like this:.

Recent findings suggest that looking at this, if the “background processing time” is the most dominant task in your operation, then isolation is the clear winner. But if serialization, plus deserialization, plus transit exceeds that cost, then there’s no need to isolate things.

And if you can’t figure out if the task is CPU-heavy or data-heavy, it certainly doesn’t hurt to measure it, for example, using performance.mark() and performance.measure() around postMessage calls to profile the transfer cost.

Miami artists’ Art Basel boycott campaign calls for alternatives to fair week’s commercial model

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December.
  • In a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December. The grassroots collective Artists 4 Artists Miami revealed plans for its “Art Basel Boycott” at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition of the Switzerland-based fair. Now, after a year of preparation, the collective is launching its first campaign, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors and residents to reconsider their participation in Miami Art Week’s fairs while building alternatives rooted in the community.

In a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair? Organisers are not calling for a blanket rejection of Miami Art Week or even its tentpole event. Instead, organisers envision a longer-term effort to challenge the economic and political structures surrounding the fair and redirect attention toward local artists, independent galleries and experimental programming.

“We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” states misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.

The campaign grew out of the collective’s broader efforts to connect cultural work with other grassroots struggles. After spending much of 2025 supporting campaigns led by other organisations, Artists 4 Artists Miami began considering how it could mobilise its own community. Its participation in protests organised by Jewish Voice for Peace and other groups opposing the war in Gaza helped crystallise the idea, soto says, prompting organisers to examine the connections between the art market, housing affordability, labour conditions, and the companies that benefit from the fair.

Sources indicate that for soto, Art Basel has become a focal point for these overlapping concerns. The fair generates significant economic activity, but the group questions how much of that value reaches Miami’s working artists and residents, particularly as the city becomes increasingly expensive. The group also points to the environmental and infrastructural costs of hosting an international event, and to the political and corporate interests associated with some of its major partners and investors.

Those concerns extend to the fair’s relationship with the city itself; soto points to a recent Miami Beach Commission decision concerning Art Basel’s rental agreement for the Miami Beach Convention Center, which reduced the fair’s rent from nearly $1m to around $500,000 and committed the equivalent of an additional $300,000 in public funds toward first-responder and security costs. The group questions whether the benefits the fair brings to the community justify the public resources devoted to it.

In a recent development, and yet, as the Artists 4 Artists Miami organisers acknowledge, Art Basel is deeply embedded in Miami’s cultural identity and economy. For many artists and arts workers, Miami Art Week provides essential income through art handling, installation, production and other contract jobs, while offering a smaller number opportunities to exhibit their work. Local galleries rely on the annual influx of collectors, press and visitors, and cultural institutions benefit from the attention and potential donor relationships the week brings.

“Art Basel Miami Beach has been a committed partner to Miami Beach and its creative community for more than two decades, supporting local artists and organisations through cultural programming, educational initiatives and opportunities for artistic exchange,” a spokesperson for Art Basel tells The Art Newspaper. “The fair also generates significant economic activity across the region, benefiting local businesses and workers in a wide range of sectors.”.

According to local officials, the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach generated nearly $60m in economic impact for the city of Miami Beach, and $570m in economic impact for Miami-Dade County. The fair has consistently included several South Florida galleries as exhibitors, and every year the city of Miami Beach acquires a work from the fair for its public art collection.

In a recent development, ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years, signed the Artists 4 Artists Miami pledge despite recognising the tensions inherent in the campaign. Lynch claims the fair offers substantial economic benefits to established galleries and collectors while providing comparatively few exhibition opportunities for local artists.

“Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach,” Lynch notes. She looks to spend Miami Art Week visiting local galleries, events and experimental exhibitions instead of attending the main fair, while introducing students to the city’s year-round art scene.

Sources indicate that still, Lynch acknowledges the difficult position facing those who depend on Art Basel for their livelihoods. For workers already struggling to make ends meet, declining paid work during Miami Art Week may not be financially feasible. That is a dilemma soto is also mindful of: the fairs have helped pay their bills and enabled them to travel internationally, but they believe the short-term benefits can obscure longer-term costs, including overwork, underappreciated labour and environmental strain.

According to recent reports, the “Art Basel Boycott” pledge is designed to accommodate different levels of participation. Signatories must select at least one commitment: not attending Art Basel Miami Beach, not exhibiting work at the fair, not exhibiting during Miami Art Week or withholding their labour from the fair. They can also choose commitments aimed at supporting alternatives, allowing participants to assess what is realistic given their circumstances.

As of this writing, the campaign had collected 21 signatures through an online form hosted on the collective’s website. Organisers are contacting local cultural and political organisations, particularly grassroots groups, to seek endorsements and establish partnerships. One existing partner is Panamía, a local network connecting businesses, creatives and residents. Artists 4 Artists Miami is also exploring programming in conjunction with a Panamía gathering and art print fair planned for Miami Art Week.

According to recent reports, beyond events, the collective hopes to establish a mutual-support network that could help pledge signatories navigate the financial consequences of opting out of Miami Art Week. That would entail connecting artists and organisations with local resources, soto indicates, including food assistance and other forms of mutual aid.

Recent findings suggest that for the boycott’s organisers and signatories, success will not necessarily be measured by a signature count or an immediate impact on the fair. Instead, they hope the campaign will encourage a gradual shift in how Miami’s cultural producers and workers understand their economic and political influence.

“If a year from now we see that much more alternative and locally focused programming happening outside of Art Week,” soto indicates, “that would be a huge victory.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

STUDIO HERRSTRÃM rebuilds the Milkshake brand identity around car culture, a redrawn splash mark, high-vis color and road signs.

In a recent development, milkshake is a Stockholm label, a division of Sony Music Entertainment founded in 2019, and its newly introduced identity starts in a car. The name was suggested on a car ride, milestones happened in cars, and new music was taken for a car test. The old splash is still there, redrawn as a rounded, blended symbol that reads like metal and liquid merging, and the wordmark runs through it with a zigzag cut that splits Milkshake into two stacked hits. On the posters the name fills the frame until the letters stop being text and start being the picture: acid yellow Milksh across the top, shake across the bottom.

In a recent development, the type system is Gates, a neo-grotesque from Contextype, shown in the specimen with arrows, asterisks, circled letters and roman numerals on a mauve field. The wordmark itself leans forward, its letters cut on a slant that matches the splash, and the supporting lockups borrow their logic from car window stickers and milk carton nutrition labels: small blocks of capitals that hold track names, release dates and the p-line symbol without breaking the grid.

The system proves itself on the objects it touches. A high-vis vest carries the full lockup on its back in black on acid yellow, with reflective bands borrowed from road markings. A neon green acrylic cube hangs outside the shopfront with the black wordmark on its face. A blender wears the whole icon set as stickers: the machine that makes the drink becomes the merch.

Sources indicate that color does the rest. Acid yellow is the signal color, while neon pink and soft lilac take the flavor cues and black keeps the contrast high. The same palette runs the subway poster for Tove Lo's single Me/You (always and forever), dated 18.09.26. Linn Wexell, founder and creative director of Milkshake, notes the creative work was smart and on point and the visuals stunning.

Weaponizing And Defending The React Flight Protocol: Deserialization Sinks In RSCs

In a recent development, durgesh Rajubhai Pawar is a freelance developer dedicated to building high-performance, accessible web applications. He specializes in orchestrating complex … More about Durgesh ↬.
