Set alerts on Google Flights for every trip you are considering in the next 6 months. You will receive email notifications when prices drop, and you can book immediately without daily searching. Google Flights date grid and Skyscanner everywhere search exist specifically to help flexible travelers find the cheapest options. Being willing to fly on a Tuesday instead of a Friday, or to visit Portugal instead of France, routinely saves 30-50% compared to fixed-date, fixed-destination searches. For FI-minded travelers, flexibility is a skill that pays dividends on every trip.

Tuesday and Wednesday are consistently the cheapest days to fly domestically, with fares typically 15-25% below Friday and Sunday prices. Saturday can also be a good value for departures. The savings are largest on popular leisure routes where weekend demand creates the biggest price swings.

Combined with a travel rewards card that earns points on everyday spending, these strategies make air travel significantly more affordable without requiring hours of research. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November). The process was part of a wider initiative by the American collector Robert McCarthy and the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio that is expected to see many more objects returned to Ethiopia.

In a recent development, mcCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art. He broadened his collection in the 1990s to include Ethiopian art, at a time when there was less concern about provenance. In 2023-24 he lent objects to the exhibition Ethiopia at the Crossroads, which was presented in venues in Baltimore, Salem in Massachusetts and Toledo. It was at Toledo that he began discussions with Sophie Ong, assistant director of strategic initiatives, about the future of his collection.

According to recent reports, ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

This eventually led to the new, complex arrangement. Toledo will acquire McCarthy’s 375 Ethiopian objects, one of the largest such private collections. Two thirds will be donated and the remainder bought. Some of this material will be exhibited when the museum’s galleries reopen in autumn 2027 after a major reinstallation of its permanent collection.

Industry observers note that the museum then intends to return much of the collection to Ethiopia, in tranches over the next 20 years. Any items deemed to have left Ethiopia illegally or inappropriately will be restituted. Details have not been released, but it is assumed that this will include looted material seized by British troops at the 1869 battle of Maqdala and which later came onto the international art market.

Industry observers note that objects judged to have been exported properly will remain at the Toledo museum. Stewardship of items with an indeterminate status will be decided jointly by the Toledo museum and Ethiopian officials. It is thought that ultimately half of McCarthy’s 375 items may be returned.

Recent findings suggest that the unusual tripartite arrangement between McCarthy, the Toledo museum and the Ethiopia authorities could prove to be a template for dealing with restitution claims by other African countries. At the handover, Alula Pankhurst, speaking on behalf of the Ethiopian Heritage Authority, described it as “a fresh model of partnership”.

In a recent development, this week’s restitution of five objects to the government’s Ethiopian Heritage Authority is slightly different, in that they have been directly returned by McCarthy. The Toledo museum was unwilling to accession them because of records suggesting that they had left Ethiopia after the 1970 Unesco convention.

In a recent development, the items are two 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and three processional crosses. All are believed to have been improperly removed from Ethiopian churches.

The earliest of the two manuscripts is a Book of Revelation with a Horologium (daily cycle of prayers). It includes seven full-page illuminations, dating from around 1400. The volume was recorded in the late 20th century as being in the Saqqā Madḫānē Ālam Church in Šawā Province.

The other manuscript is a large mid-15th century Gospels, which includes full-page images of the Four Evangelists. The scholar Diana Spencer noted in a 1974 article that she saw it at the church of Emmaus Giyor near Wafa Yasus.

Sources indicate that ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

Recent findings suggest that the three brass processional crosses being returned date variously from the late-18th to early-20th centuries. Each has incised inscriptions which may make it possible to determine which church they came from.

According to recent reports, the five returned objects are now being sent from London to the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa, where a upcoming display of restituted material is scheduled to open in December. Most of the rest of the display will be material which had been looted at Maqdala.

However, the forthcoming Addis Ababa display may feed into a debate over whether religious items that can be identified with a particular location should be retained in the National Museum or returned to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Naming is hard. The language we use shapes the way we think about things, but also the conversation we have about it. That’s why we have so much confusion about colors, icons, UI components, features — and that’s why we struggle to name design tokens, HTML classes, and variables.

It has been revealed that sometimes, the names we choose are too generic, so it’s difficult to understand what exactly is meant. And sometimes they are too specific, leaving little room for flexibility and reuse. How do we choose the right names? And which naming conventions work best? Let’s take a closer look.

If you’re looking for some inspiration for naming HTML classes, CSS properties, or JavaScript functions, Classnames is a wonderful resource jam-packed with ideas that get you thinking outside the box.

Industry observers note that the site provides thematically grouped lists of words perfect for naming. You’ll find terms to describe different kinds of behavior, likeness between things, order, grouping, and association, but also themed collections of words that wouldn’t instantly come to one’s mind when it comes to code, among them words from nature, art, theater, music, architecture, fashion, and publishing.

It has been revealed that how would you choose the right name for a given color? Fortunately, David Aerne maintains a tremendous repository of color names, presently with 30355 unique color names, sourced from various references and 1000s of user contributions.

Sources indicate that of course, the repository comes with a color picker and name search and plenty of other color pickers as well. Tremendous work, which is also a fantastic reference to keep nearby.

What makes a good name? Javier Cuello summarized a set of naming best practices that help you name your layers, groups, and components in a consistent and scalable way.

It has been revealed that as Javier points out, a good name has a logical structure, is short, meaningful, known by everyone, and not related to visual properties. He shares do’s and don’ts to illustrate how to achieve that and also takes a closer look at all the fine little details you need to consider when naming sizes, colors, groups, layers, and components.

How to build a flexible design token taxonomy that works across different products? That was the challenge that the team at Intuit faced. The parent tech giant of products such as Mailchimp, QuickBooks, TurboTax, and Mint developed a flexible token system that goes beyond the brand theme to serve as the foundational system for a wide array of products.

Nate Baldwin wrote a case study in which he shares valuable insights into the making of Intuit’s design token taxonomy. It dives deeper into the pain points of the old taxonomy system, the criteria they defined for the fresh system, and how it was created. Lots of takeaways for building your own robust and flexible token taxonomy are guaranteed.

Looking at what other people call similar things is a great way to start when you’re struggling with naming. And what better source could there be than other design systems? Before you end up in the design system rabbit hole, Iain Bean did the research for you and created the Component Gallery.

According to recent reports, it’s a collection that includes plenty of examples for more than 50 UI components — from accordion to visually hidden — and also lists other names that the UI components go by. A fantastic resource, and not only with regard to naming.

According to recent reports, features often have low adoption due to poor discoverability. Feature adoption needs time — first the feature must be discovered, then understood, then tried, learned, and eventually built into existing workflow. Erin Gannon has written a helpful practical guide on how to make sure all of it happens.

Recent findings suggest that good names are driven by user needs and problems. They should signal the value or outcome of a feature (the job-to-be-done), and — most importantly! — tap into the user’s own language. So ask people to explain a feature in their own words and then use the words they use.

According to recent reports, A wonderful example of naming guidelines for a complex multi-brand, multi-themed design system comes from the Vodafone UK Design System team. Their Variables Taxonomy Map breaks down the anatomy and categorization of a design token into a well-orchestrated system of collections.

The map illustrates four collections required to support the system and connections between tokens — from brand and primitives to semantics and pages. It builds on top of Nathan Curtis’ work on naming design tokens and enables everyone to gather insight about where a token is used and what it represents, just from its name.

If you want to explore more approaches to naming design tokens, I’ve put together a list of useful Figma kits and resources that are worth checking out.

Romina Kavcic created a helpful little tool for naming design tokens — from learning how they work and how to name them well to configuring your own naming structure with components, categories, states, and roles.

If you are looking for the right name for your product or service, Onym is a fantastic open-source repository that organizes tools and resources for finding names for brainstorming, vetting, guides, sprints, etymologies — all the way to cautionary tales and agencies that name things, as well as useful books to take a look at.

A quick-reference list of tools and guides for naming just about… well, anything, in one place:.

Sources indicate that the right name is the one that’s well-understood and used by the team and customers. So much time is wasted speaking about the very same thing but in different dialects — the designer’s dialect, the developer’s dialect, the product manager’s dialect, and the user’s dialect. That’s what often causes frustration and confusion.

So if you see low adoption, it might be merely because of the name. And pay attention to potential naming conflicts and put them in a backlog of things to address later. It’s one of those fine little details that can reduce frustration and confusion and help teams work together better.

In a recent development, we hope you’ll find these wonderful projects useful — put together by wonderful creators. A friendly shout-out to everyone sharing their work with folks to use and learn from! That’s one of the reasons why we truly love the web and people building and designing it. 💚.

We love seeing what we all can do to make the web more accessible and usable. Pentagram rebuilds Poetry Foundationâs brand identity around a redrawn Pegasus mark, central-axis type stacks, and two-color covers.

In a recent development, seventy black silhouettes sit in neat rows on off-white paper, tracing how Pentagram stripped a century-old winged horse down to one sharp mark. Since 1912, the Pegasus has belonged primarily to Poetry magazine, the Chicago journal that early on printed Gwendolyn Brooks, Carl Sandburg, and T. S. Eliot. Pentagramâs brief was to turn that single emblem into a unified brand identity for the entire Poetry Foundation. It isnât treated like a fragile crest locked in a corner. On the black lockup sheet, the Pegasus rides between wide-tracked POETRY and FOUNDATION lettering, tops 2026 Pegasus Awards, shrinks into an inline paragraph bullet, and tucks beside the numerals 61. One silhouette carries the organization across every scale.

According to recent reports, photography steps out of the frame here. As Pentagram notes, poetsâ words become the artwork, anchored by a central-axis stacking motif built so the internal team can assemble layouts rapidly. The black scale diagram maps that range from a clean Meet Our Grantee-Partner: header into a dense mission block where tiny uppercase lines weave between oversized serifs. The cover system doesnât hide the writing inside. On the cobalt-blue issue, hot-pink display type pulls KB Brookinsâs line, Give me more to immortalize, straight to the front beneath a pink orb â nodding to the magazineâs founding âOpen Doorâ policy. Across fourteen consecutive spines from January 2026 through May 2028, each issue pairs two contrasting inks with a tiny Pegasus at the base, while the brown back cover centers electric-blue poet names above a five-Pegasus arc.

Beyond print, the brand identity loosens up without losing structure. On a white wall clock set over wood paneling, twelve black Pegasus silhouettes replace the hour numerals in mid-flight poses. Everyday objects follow suit. A natural canvas tote stacks The poets have emerged! in chunky black serifs beneath a small MAGAZINE lockup, and an oatmeal cap with a forest-green corduroy brim tucks an embroidered Pegasus and Poetry above the bill. Inside, open spreads like Koko Taylor Is the Healer of Wounded Women give poems calm serif pacing and wide margins, while the Poetry Off the Shelf podcast tile brings the rust-red mark onto mobile. #115335. Van Gogh’s record-breaking ‘Blossoming Chestnut Trees’: the $190m sale and the restitution claim that nearly upended it

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1345 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Van Gogh’s record-breaking ‘Blossoming Chestnut Trees’: the $190m sale and the restitution claim that nearly upended it

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's New York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees.
  • Sources indicate that the auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in.
  • It has been revealed that before the auction, Sotheby’s had not confirmed a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's New York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees. Auctioneer Oliver Barker began the sale by stating that “the work is being offered for sale pursuant to an agreement between the seller and the heirs of the Hedwig and Samuel Fischer family”. The Fischer family had sold the painting in 1936.

Sources indicate that the auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in. A third bidder, in the saleroom, won the contest after less than four minutes, at a hammer price of $165m. He is the Fresh York dealer William Acquavella, presumably acting for an unidentified client.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (May 1890).

It has been revealed that before the auction, Sotheby’s had not confirmed a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees). This may have been slightly optimistic, since it was far more than any Van Gogh has ever made. Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890) is a fine landscape, although not among his very best. And the other 11 pictures in last night’s auction of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection generally sold for around, or even below, their lower estimates.

Industry observers note that the uncertainty last weekend over a possible Nazi-era claim for the Van Gogh may have discouraged some potential bidders, but the $190m (including fees) was nonetheless an astonishing result. This was for an artist who had failed to sell during his own lifetime. Van Gogh completed nearly a thousand paintings in his career, with only a single recorded sale: The Red Vineyard (November 1888, Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow).

Only three artworks have ever sold for more at auction: Leonardo’s Salvator Mundi (around 1500, $450m, Christie’s, 2017), Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1916, $236m, Sotheby’s, 2025) and Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn (1964, $195m, Christie’s, 2022).

In a recent development, the previous record price for a Van Gogh was $117m (including fees) for Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888), which Christie’s sold in 2022. The Blossoming Chestnut Trees price was 62% more.

Sources indicate that sotheby’s has been open about Blossoming Chestnut Trees’s Nazi-era (1933-45) provenance. Following our inquiries, we reported in our 2 October blog post: “It was purchased four years later [in 1926] by the Berlin-based publisher Samuel Fischer, and on his death in 1934 it passed to his daughter Brigitte. Although the family was persecuted because of their Jewish heritage, a Sotheby’s spokesperson confirmed to us that, based on recent research, the family was free at all times to dispose of the painting.”.

Literaturport.de via Wikimedia Commons.

News of a possible Nazi-era claim emerged only five weeks later. Berlin-based Gunnar Schnabel, who describes himself as a “looted art researcher” specialising in the Nazi period, told the Fresh York Times that he first heard about the sale on 7 November, when he was “lying on a sofa in his vacation home”. His letter to Sotheby’s calling for the sale to be delayed was sent on 12 November, just six days before the auction. Obviously this put Sotheby’s in a very awkward situation: should the sale be postponed or go ahead?

In response, Sotheby’s stated: “We are aware of the persecution experienced by the Fischer family. After the Anschluss in 1938, the family fled Austria, and the Gestapo confiscated their Vienna home, library and remaining art collection. But the circumstances around this transaction were different”. The auction house also added that after the war, no claim was ever made for the Van Gogh.

Urgent negotiations were held with the representatives of the Fischer family. The key question at stake was whether their ancestors had been the victim of a forced sale at a lower than market value. By June 1936, when the Van Gogh was sold, the family had just moved to Vienna. They had consigned the painting to the Cassirer gallery in Amsterdam several years earlier, in 1932-33. The price eventually paid in 1936 by the buyer, Paris-based collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer, was $22,000.

It has been revealed that comparisons with other Van Gogh sales around the time are telling. In 1935, the year before the Fischer sale, Orchard with Cypresses had sold for $15,000 at the New York auction house Parke Bernet (this was the painting which later fetched a record Van Gogh price in 2022). That makes the $22,000 seem reasonable.

Then there is the Sunflowers (August 1888), which had been sold to London's National Gallery in 1924 for the equivalent of $5,800. Although this sale took place 12 years before Blossoming Chestnut Trees and Jo Bonger, Vincent’s sister-in-law, probably reduced the price for a major museum, it is now regarded as Van Gogh’s greatest masterpiece. This again suggests that the Fischers received a reasonable sum for their picture.

Following yesterday’s Sotheby’s auction, Schnabel told The Art Newspaper that the Fischers had also been supported by the Commission for Looted Art in Europe's co-chair Anne Webber. He added that the family is delighted that Blossoming Chestnut Trees “which hung in the Berlin home of Samuel and Hedwig Fischer for a quarter of a century, has now found a fresh owner”. They hope this case “may offer some encouragement to other families who have faced persecution during the Nazi era, and that they, too, may find a path toward the recognition of their rightful claims.”.

It has been revealed that the terms of the 17 November settlement between the heirs of the Fischer family and the Blaquier-Arrieta family remain confidential. Presumably some sort of financial compensation has been paid. The agreement opens the door for the Fischer heirs to make claims for further paintings which had once been in their family if they come onto the market in the future.

Title page of the Leicester Galleries exhibition Artists who Died Young, with an image of Blossoming Chestnut Trees.

According to recent reports, as a postscript on the 1930s story of Blossoming Chestnut Trees, soon after the Kapferers bought the picture they lent it to an exhibition in London, Artists who Died Young at the Leicester Galleries in 1938. A year after the London exhibition, war broke out. Blossoming Chestnut Trees had been sent to the United States a few months earlier to New York dealers Wildenstein & Co and, after passing through two American private collections, it went to Argentina in 1975, to the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Following the Sotheby’s sale, it remains a mystery where the Van Gogh will ultimately reside.

In a recent development, martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin Bailey’s recent Van Gogh books.

In a recent development, martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

According to recent reports, his other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com.

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

#115334. Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2070 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • It has been revealed that the way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking. He has over 25 years experience working with clients such as Doctors … More about Paul ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that the way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy. If it were turned into a movie, reviewers would say it was unbelievable. Nobody could be that stupid.

In a recent development, yet here we are. And what makes it all the more frustrating is that we have been here before.

In a recent development, back in 2014, I wrote a book for Smashing Magazine called Digital Adaptation, looking at the mistakes being made in how organizations were approaching digital transformation and what they should be doing instead. The similarities between then and now are striking.

So in this post, I want to look back at Digital Adaptation and see how the lessons in that book apply to the AI era and what we can learn from the past to help us navigate the challenges of AI today.

The biggest mistake, both then and now, is approaching each as a technological challenge.

Recent findings suggest that sure, both digital transformation and AI are technological advances, and yes, some level of technological implementation is required. But that is the tip of a very large iceberg.

Recent findings suggest that back in the midst of the digital transformation era, IT departments were rolling out CMSs, CRM systems, intranets, and so on. Meanwhile, on the customer-facing side, organizations were rolling out websites, apps, and personalization. But they were putting almost no emphasis on how people were going to use these systems.

Internal systems were hard to use, and customers either didn’t care what was being built or wanted something else entirely.

In a recent development, the same is happening with AI. Senior management are buying into the hype, and IT teams are rolling out Copilot Studio licenses manufacturer-wide and considering the job done. Sure, there is a bit of organization-wide generic training, but that’s about it.

Just like before, staff are left wondering what to do with these new systems and feeling under pressure to use them and deliver results.

In a recent development, after all, this time around, it is even worse, because this time, staff fear for their jobs. They have read the same headlines that you have, and no amount of promises from senior management is going to make them feel any better.

I mean, think about it from a staff member’s point of view. AI offers them very little personally, even setting aside the fact that management may be intending to use it to replace them.

Recent findings suggest that the main reason senior management are excited about AI is that it provides additional productivity. People can do more in less time. But that does not benefit staff. They are still required to work 9 to 5, but now they are expected to do more in the same time. They don’t get any time back, and they don’t get paid more, so why would they embrace AI?

One strategy is to help staff identify the parts of their job they hate and how AI can help them do those tasks more rapidly and less painfully. People tend to be a lot more receptive to change when it is presented as an opportunity to improve their working lives.

But, that should just be the beginning. Organizations may need to consider providing incentives for staff to adopt AI in terms of career progression, compensation, or shorter working hours.

Also, adopting AI is not a simple task. It involves challenging every working practice they have built up over (in some cases) decades. All of that procedural knowledge has to be rebuilt. That is a lot to ask of anybody in even the best of circumstances, and most employees do not find themselves in the best of circumstances.

Most are overworked and struggling to stay on top of their to-do lists. They don’t have time to sit down, learn a upcoming tool, and figure out how it fits into their workflow.

That doesn’t just take time. It also takes a lot of consideration and experimentation. It is not enough to just send a member of staff on a training course and expect them to be able to use AI to its full potential.

In a recent development, at a minimum, staff need training specific to their roles, such as the AI training I provide to UX teams. But organizations should be going even further.

They need to develop sophisticated training programs that help staff from different departments understand how to use AI in their specific roles. They need ongoing support and the time to experiment with AI to find the best ways to use it.

But formal training will only take you so far. In my experience, the most effective support comes from colleagues, which is why I would start with the enthusiasts rather than the resisters. Every organization has a handful of people who are already experimenting with AI, often without anybody asking them to. Bring those people together, give them the time and space to share what is working for them, and let their enthusiasm spread to everyone else.

It has been revealed that I saw this work during the digital transformation era too. In Digital Adaptation, I described an internal conference where staff showed their colleagues what they had built, and it did more for adoption than any memo from the top ever could. People are far more likely to try something when they see a colleague in a similar role using it successfully than when they are told to by senior management.

Unfortunately, experimentation comes with a substantial downside… mistakes will be made.

In a recent development, many organizations have, to be frank, a culture of fear where mistakes are seen as a sign of incompetence. However, by its very nature, learning a new tool like AI will involve making mistakes, and this can be a massive barrier to adoption.

According to recent reports, I saw this during the era of digital transformation. Senior management would demand digital transformation and were confused when it didn’t happen.

What they didn’t realize was that they were sending mixed messages to staff. Sure, they were asking for digital transformation, but they were still demanding that the same key performance indicators (KPIs) be met, and they still pointed out any mistakes in their annual reviews.

There was no space to fail, as the pressure to deliver was relentless.

In a recent development, this time around, it seems to be even worse. I hear horror stories of staff being reprimanded for using too many tokens just weeks after being told to adopt AI. Or staff being lectured so much about what they should or should not do with AI that they are afraid to try anything. It is safer to just do what they have always done.

Recent findings suggest that look, I get it. AI cannot be rolled out without some governance in place, but again, this is an area that organizations have typically handled poorly.

In the midst of digital transformation, governance would either be non-existent, or it would be so strict that it would stifle innovation, and unfortunately, I see the same pattern emerging with AI adoption.

Sources indicate that staff need some governance to help them know where they stand. It helps them understand what is expected of them and what they can and cannot do.

Recent findings suggest that but too often organizations have been so strict that it is easier not to do anything at all. Pages of instructions about what people should and should not share with AI create that sense of fear that I mentioned earlier.

Of course, mistakes will get made, but that is the cost of change, and so organizations need to accept that and do what they can to mitigate that in how they roll out the technology.

That said, organizations will need to be careful in how they roll out AI from an IT perspective. Once again, it is easy to lock everything down and stifle the adoption of AI.

Again, this is something I highlighted back in 2014 with digital transformation. Overstretched IT teams would pick a set of technologies and roll them out organization-wide, often with little or no consultation with the individuals who would be using them. Anything outside of that set of technologies had to go through a complex approval process, normally involving a steering committee. The result was a glacial pace of change that was one of the major contributing factors to the failure rate of digital transformation projects.

Today we are seeing the same thing. IT teams are opting into a tool like Copilot and calling it a day, but that often falls massively short.

Take, for example, a UX team I am working with at the moment. Management is pushing hard for AI adoption, and the team is excited about the potential of creating an AI-powered research repository and even AI personas. It sounds like a wonderful case study in AI adoption, with enthusiastic management, an excited team, and innovative ideas.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, the reality is that nothing is happening because Copilot cannot deliver on the team’s vision, and so they are right now bogged down in bureaucracy as they try to persuade the AI steering group that they need to use a different toolset. Understandably, the team’s enthusiasm is waning. Why bother?

Industry observers note that and that team is one of the more patient ones. In many organizations, staff are not waiting for the steering group at all. Just as we saw shadow IT during the digital transformation era, with people signing up for Dropbox and Google Docs because the official tools could not do what they needed, we are now seeing shadow AI. When the in-house AI tool will not let people do their jobs, they open a personal ChatGPT or Claude account on their phone or home laptop and get on with it.

It has been revealed that that is far more dangerous than the problem the restrictions were meant to prevent. Manufacturer data ends up in tools the organization has no control over, with no oversight and no record of what has been shared. In trying to lock everything down, organizations end up pushing the risk somewhere they cannot see it.

Recent findings suggest that the instinctive reaction is to clamp down with stricter policies, blocked websites, and warnings about disciplinary action. But that rarely works, and it drives the behavior further underground. Shadow AI is a symptom, and a useful one, because it reveals exactly where the official tools are falling short.

It has been revealed that look, I understand the cost of a messy, out-of-control tech stack. It is not ideal. However, in the early days of adoption, we may have to live with a bit of chaos while people explore the edges of what is possible and work out common use cases.

Industry observers note that organizations need to allow staff to explore different uses of AI and even different AI apps to find what suits their specific needs in their specific roles. They can always start locking things down later as the real organizational needs become clearer.

I admit all of this feels dangerous to some organizations. They want to control the AI adoption process centrally and make sure nothing goes wrong. I understand that. But change comes with a degree of risk, and the risk of moving too slowly is greater than the risk of moving too fast.

Industry observers note that however, a bigger danger still is when organizations see this as a technological challenge and overlook the human side of things. AI adoption is not simply about rolling out new technology. Just like digital transformation, it is about people, culture, and change management. The sooner organizations realize the scope of what they are dealing with, the better.

Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that brecht De Ruyte is a self-taught front-end developer located in Belgium with a passion for UX and Design. After more than a decade of working in tech, he … More about Brecht ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment. But when I heard that the native CSS random() function landed in Safari and is rolling out in Chrome 156, I started wondering: where does randomness actually make sense on the web? Is it something we want in our design system? To find out, I did what I always do in doubt: I built a bunch of playful CodePen demos exploring organic typography, bouncing letters, splayed cards, and a punk fanzine.

According to recent reports, as someone who loves building design systems and tinkering with CSS architecture, a massive part of my day job revolves around control. We set up spacing scales, lock down typography, set up color tokens, and make sure everything aligns on a grid. Consistency is usually our bread and butter as design engineers and a proud badge of skill when creating design systems. If a card suddenly jumps 20 pixels to the left on a refresh, it’s not creative expression; it’s a bug that the project manager will log.

So when I first heard that the native random() function from the CSS Values and Units Level 5 spec was shipped in Safari, and is presently rolling out in Chrome 156 (with positive signals from Mozilla on Firefox as well), my first reaction was: that’s pretty cool!

And my second reaction was: wait… where would I actually use this without making a mess? How can I convince designers that random might be a good idea for a design system?

According to recent reports, because let’s be honest: why on earth would we want randomness in our stylesheets when we’ve spent the last decade trying to make the web more predictable? Even when using flexbox or fluid typography, we’re still trying to make things as aligned and uniform as possible.

If you step away from the browser for a second and look at physical things around you, nothing is ever truly uniform.

Take an old letterpress print: the ink bleeds slightly into the paper grain, some letters have a microscopic tilt, and the baseline isn’t always that straight. Or think about a deck of Polaroid photos dropped on a coffee table; those photos aren’t perfect, probably not straight either. Or what about lights flickering in a street at night? That little bit of analog messiness is what makes things feel alive, organic, and human.

Sources indicate that on the web, we’ve gotten so good at pixel perfection that sometimes our interfaces end up feeling a bit sterile. We notice this even more now with rapidly created designs by an unguided LLM; we usually end up with the same sort of design we had 10 years ago. Everything is squared off, aligned, neat. It works, but frankly, it does get a bit boring.

In a recent development, randomness in CSS doesn’t have to mean throwing your design system out the window. It’s about little imperfections and playfulness. Maybe let’s even call it fun.

To see what this actually looks like in practice, I spent a few hours tinkering in CodePen. The demos might feel a bit isolated, but I’m sure that many designers could make the best of this controlled chaos. But before we look at those demos, let’s take a look at the syntax.

According to recent reports, the random() function is specified in CSS Values and Units Module Level 5. It generates a pseudo-random value inside your CSS without needing JavaScript or a build-time Sass loop.

The formal specification looks like this:.

In practice, and across current browser implementations, you can just write comma-separated arguments:.

It won’t be a shocker for most people, but I thought I should at least mention that your minimum and maximum bounds must share the exact same unit type.

The CSS parser needs to know what dimension it’s dealing with. You can use lengths, angles, time, percentages, or plain unitless numbers:.

If you ever need to combine units, you’ll have to reach for calc() inside the arguments so each side resolves properly.

According to recent reports, the optional third argument is the step size. If you don’t add it, the browser picks from a continuous range. But if you provide a step, it rounds the random value to discrete increments:.

This can be helpful in cases where you want things to jump around a bit, but you still want them to land on your pre-defined grid.

According to recent reports, normally, every time random() is evaluated on a property, it creates an independent random value. But there could be an example where you create a box that sets inline-size and block-size at random, but at the same time you need them to match so the element stays a perfect square.

That’s where the caching key comes in:.

In the latest spec, a bare dashed ident like --square-size shares its seed globally across every element in the document (which would make all cards identical). To keep width and height linked on a single element while giving each card its own independent size, the spec requires pairing it with the element-scoped keyword (e.g. --square-size element-scoped).

Industry observers note that to see this in action, I created a little example. In the top row, the tiles have uncached dimensions, which distorts each tile into an unpredictable, mismatched rectangle. In the bottom row, both inline-size and block-size share --square-size, guaranteeing that each tile remains a pristine 1:1 square. Refresh the CodePen a couple of times and notice the bottom cards keeping the same randomness:.

See the Pen [Uncached vs cached random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e91-4bac-765e-b04e-a53636759163) by @utilitybend.

Because we’re still in the rollout phase, you’ll want to wrap your experiments in @supports:.

Industry observers note that there’s also another function in the spec called random-item(). While random() handles numerical ranges, random-item() lets you pick from a list of predefined tokens or keywords:.

In a recent development, this can be handy to randomise from a set of design tokens. This one does not have any browser support at the moment, but it certainly is something to look forward to.

And now for the practical part.

According to recent reports, when I started playing with the feature, I was also doing some typography tricks with animations. So that’s where my first thought went: Typography! What if we just add a tiny bit of imperfection to a word?

It has been revealed that think of vintage book covers. The letters aren’t misaligned by miles, but they have small imperfections.

See the Pen [Imperfection random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-157f-708d-a704-fa067114aaca) by @utilitybend.

Here is the CSS powering the letters:.

Sources indicate that I also added a little hover effect. While you’re reading, the word feels playful. But the second you hover over it, every character snaps back.

Sources indicate that one quick accessibility warning here: If you break a word into separate elements so you can style each letter, screen readers will often read it out as individual characters: “i - m - p - e - r - f - e - c - t - i - o - n”, or pause awkwardly between each one. That’s a terrible user experience.

Always hide the visual spans from assistive tech and provide the full word:.

Screen reader owners get the clean text, and sighted users get the fun visual quirks.

Once I had those letters sitting there with their little tilts, I couldn’t resist: what if we animated it?

I started tinkering with a bounce keyframe. I was just goofing around, but the end result gave me a little smile. If you animate every letter with the exact same timing, you get that clean sine wave we’ve all seen before. But if every letter gets its own jump height, its own duration, and its own landing squash, suddenly the word looks like a bunch of little characters jumping around on a trampoline.

See the Pen [Bouncy imperfection with CSS random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-c117-729f-9844-ddf19fc1fc96) by @utilitybend.

Here is how the bounce parameters are wired up:.

Notice the negative animation delay (--delay: random(-3s, 0s)).

Industry observers note that if you set a positive delay, the letters sit frozen on page load, waiting for their timers to expire before jumping. By using a negative delay, the browser pretends the animation has already been running for a few seconds. The moment the page loads, every letter is already bouncing at its own rhythm.

We’ve built cards. Lots of cards. So many cards… Portfolio grids, blog summaries, feature lists. And most of the time, they sit in three or four neat, boring columns.

For dashboards, that’s exactly what you want. But if you’re building a lifestyle portfolio, a children’s website, or a collection of vacation photos, we can be a bit more playful. In the following example, I did just that:.

See the Pen [Random card tilt [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e93-849d-72a9-9254-3f4305e58a34) by @utilitybend.

Here’s how I put that together:.

Industry observers note that in the example, playing around with the shadow was a fun experiment. I will probably try more effects with that in the future.

Here is where modern CSS features start getting really interesting. In the previous demo with tilting cards, we used pure randomness. But what if you have a stack of cards that needs to fan out across the screen as you scroll?

In this example, I decided to use math for the structure and randomness for the human imperfection.

See the Pen [Scroll drivin animations with random() tilted cards [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e94-79c6-70b1-97d4-66b7c2d736b0) by @utilitybend.

Look at how cleanly this works:.

If you’ve ever looked at brutalist or high-end fashion websites, you’ve probably seen horizontal marquee text drifting across the screen as you scroll down the page.

Usually, you see developers creating classes like .drift-slow, .drift-fast, .drift-reverse, or using a hefty JavaScript scroll listener to compute transforms.

With random() and a tiny bit of math, we can get procedural drift speeds in just a few lines:.

See the Pen [Random() velocity scroll animation [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-4cbe-77bd-9128-685d2c75cc56) by @utilitybend.

Industry observers note that calc(pow(-1, sibling-index())) gives us alternating directions (1, -1, 1, -1), and random(15%, 44%) decides how fast each row travels. As you scroll, each typographic line moves at its own tempo.

Recent findings suggest that I love photography, and one of my favorite things about prime lenses is shallow depth of field. When you shoot at a wide aperture like f/1.7, only whatever is right on your focal plane stays sharp. Everything else melts away into soft bokeh. Yep, photography is all about that bokeh!

By combining random() with filter: blur(), opacity, and scale, we can recreate that lens feel:.

See the Pen [All about that random() bokeh [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-fe50-76dc-943b-d75fcaf704e6) by @utilitybend.

Some words land at blur(0px) with full opacity right in front of your eyes. Others blur out to 6px or 8px and fade into the background. And when you hover over any blurry item in the back, it rack-focuses right into sharpness. It’s a great little effect for decorative hero sections or tag clouds.

Now that we’ve played with the wild side, let’s talk about where this actually belongs in our daily work.

But! I am happy to be proven wrong here. I encourage you to challenge the status quo and experiment with this.

Any time you use animations, you have to respect user preferences for reduced motion:.

It has been revealed that if someone prefers reduced motion, it could also be a good idea to flatten the angles, not just the animations. I can imagine that a lot of random angles can also upset people while scrolling. Design should be fun, but never at the cost of accessibility.

Tinkering with random() over the last couple of days was a lot of fun. I’m still not sure if I’ll be able to convince my designer friends, but what I do know is that it brings a bit of joy.

Whenever we wanted a bit of organic randomness on the web, we had to make compromises: either pull in a JavaScript animation library, or write huge preprocessor loops that spit out hundreds of lines of static CSS. Having this built into the browser engine with zero JavaScript overhead is such a welcome addition.

It has been revealed that we spent the last decade mastering consistency, tokens, and design systems. Now that we have that foundation in place, maybe it’s time to let a little bit of playful messiness back onto the web.

I really believe that the web is supposed to be fun.

Never mind the defaults; here is CSS random().

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world? The latest Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 report, which surveyed 3,100 high net-worth individuals (HNWIs) who collect art, reveals that social media platforms—and Instagram in particular—are an increasingly key tool for discovering art and artists, buying works and promoting collections. Here is how online platforms are being used and what the art world can learn from it.

While the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media. Interestingly, online channels were a less common route into collecting for Gen Z collectors (10%) than for Gen X (16%), “running against any assumption that younger collectors might be more likely to find their way to collecting through digital channels”, the report says.

Industry observers note that the data also shows that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas. “While being introduced to art through family or cultural exposure may reflect a more passive route into collecting, those who started out online were typically more active in seeking out art content,” the report indicates. “This suggests a more deliberate, self-directed collecting journey that carries forward into greater engagement with events later on.”.

Industry observers note that when it comes to collecting, 58% of respondents noted they had used digital resources for advice with 32% of collectors citing either Instagram or X (formerly Twitter) as sources when it came to making purchases. Nineteen percent used recommendations from Instagram (up 2% year-on-year), including 22% of Gen Z respondents, and women were more likely to use them than men. The platform X—which has seen decreased usage in recent years due to controversies around its ownership and usage—was used by 18% of the sample, and this was again highest among Gen Z (23%).

A collectors’ likeliness to use social media recommendations for collecting also depended greatly on where a person was from: collectors in Hong Kong, the US and the UK were most likely to use social media for advice while those in Mainland China were less likely, undoubtedly due to the restrictions of social media platforms in the country.

Contrary to popular belief around the slow uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in the art world, the study also showed that collectors trusted AI tools for art recommendations twice as much as those from social media and influencers, and also slightly more than in-store advisors and editorial content.

The importance of ​​online and social media platforms in reaching collectors is growing. According to the survey, 27% of HNWIs’ total expenditure was made through such external platforms, up by 5 percentage points year-on-year and from 17% in 2024. The share of collectors buying directly from artists also grew to 69%, with 38% of works bought via Instagram, highlighting the benefits of a strong, independent social media presence for artists. It is also interesting to note that artist-direct spending through Instagram was higher among newly introduced collectors than more experienced ones: 8% for those in the market for two years or less, versus just 2% for those collecting for 20 years or more.

It has been revealed that but can seeing a work online really seal the deal? Apparently so—among the 75% of respondents who had purchased a work directly from a dealer in 2025/2026, 53% had bought via Instagram without viewing the work in person, up from 43% in 2024.

The report interestingly states that the youngest generation of collectors—Gen Z—are not the ones using social media the most in their collecting journeys. “The generation raised on social media is, it turns out, the one most inclined to keep its collecting close,” the report says. While the data revealed that Gen Z were the highest-spending generation surveyed and had the most wide-ranging collecting habits, their awareness of digital footprints leads them to seek greater control and privacy over their "personal and cultural identities".

“Anonymous accounts and smaller, niche social networking platforms allow them to communicate in ways that feel less pressurised and performative,” the report states. “With social media feeds heavily controlled and populated by algorithms rather than personal networks, Gen Z consumers are increasingly interested in taking back control over who sees their personal content by sharing it with smaller, vetted and carefully chosen audiences.”.

When it came to sharing information about their collections with the wider public, only 25% Gen Z shared their own content publicly, compared with 36% of millennials and around one third of other older collectors.

In a recent development, most estate planning advice assumes you will work until 60-65, accumulate wealth gradually, and have employer-provided benefits until Medicare kicks in. The FIRE path breaks every one of those assumptions. You may stop working at 35, 40, or 50 — meaning your estate plan must cover a potentially 40 to 50-year retirement, not the 20 to 25-year retirement conventional planning addresses.

This extended timeline creates unique vulnerabilities:.

The SECURE Act fundamentally changed how inherited retirement accounts work, and this change matters enormously for FIRE households that have built large tax-advantaged portfolios.

Before the SECURE Act, non-spouse beneficiaries could "stretch" inherited IRA distributions over their own lifetime, allowing decades of tax-deferred growth. Now, most non-spouse beneficiaries must withdraw the entire inherited IRA balance within 10 years of the original owner's death. For a beneficiary in their peak earning years, this compressed timeline can push them into the 32% or 37% tax bracket on every distribution.

The FIRE advantage: Early retirees have years — sometimes decades — of lower taxable income between leaving work and taking Social Security or required minimum distributions. This creates a golden window for Roth conversions that no conventional retiree has.

It has been revealed that A married couple who retires at 40 with $1.5 million in a traditional 401(k) and a $500,000 Roth IRA could systematically convert $80,000 to $100,000 per year from the traditional to the Roth, staying within the 22% bracket. Over 15 years, they convert $1.2 million to $1.5 million at a known, relatively low tax rate. Their heirs then inherit a Roth IRA that is completely tax-free — even under the SECURE Act's 10-year distribution rule.

According to recent reports, without conversions, those heirs would owe ordinary income tax on every dollar withdrawn from the inherited traditional IRA, potentially at 32% or higher if they are working professionals during their peak earning years. The tax savings for heirs can easily exceed $200,000 to $400,000 on a $1.5 million inherited traditional IRA.

In a recent development, key Roth inheritance rule: Inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to the 10-year distribution rule, but the distributions are tax-free. The 10-year clock starts the year after the original owner's death.

Sources indicate that A revocable living trust is the foundational estate planning tool for FIRE households. It provides three critical benefits that matter more for early retirees than conventional retirees:.

Every early retiree needs three healthcare documents executed before leaving their employer:.

Once you cross the $1 million net worth threshold — common in the FIRE community — asset protection becomes essential. You have decades of retirement ahead during which a lawsuit, car accident judgment, or liability claim could threaten the wealth you worked so hard to build.

For FIRE households pursuing charitable giving, a donor-advised fund (DAF) allows you to front-load charitable deductions in high-income years (or Roth conversion years), reduce your taxable estate, and distribute grants to charities over time. A DAF contribution is irrevocable and immediately reduces your estate while giving you advisory control over future grants.

Do not wait until traditional retirement age to complete your estate initiative. The moment you leave employer benefits, you need a fully executed will or trust, healthcare directives, powers of attorney, updated beneficiary designations, and umbrella insurance. Many FIRE retirees leave their jobs with $1 million or more in assets and no estate plan in place. Every day without these documents is a day your family is exposed to probate, court-appointed guardianship, and preventable tax consequences.

Absolutely. If you have any assets, dependents, or strong preferences about medical care, you need at least a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney. If you have reached FI with $500,000 or more in assets, a revocable living trust adds significant value through probate avoidance and incapacity protection.

It has been revealed that most non-spouse beneficiaries must now withdraw the entire inherited IRA or 401(k) within 10 years of the original owner's death. This compressed timeline can push heirs into high tax brackets. Roth conversions during your lifetime eliminate this tax burden because inherited Roth IRA distributions are tax-free.

For most early retirees, transferring your primary residence to a revocable living trust makes sense. It avoids probate on the home, enables seamless management if you become incapacitated, and does not affect your mortgage, property tax, or homestead exemption in most states. Consult your estate attorney about your state's specific rules.

Umbrella insurance provides liability coverage above the limits of your auto and homeowners policies. A $1 million umbrella policy typically costs $200 to $300 per year and protects against lawsuits, car accident judgments, and liability claims that exceed your underlying policy limits. For FIRE households with significant assets, it is one of the most cost-effective forms of protection available.

Yes, and early retirement is often the best time to do them. With no employment income, your taxable income is low, allowing you to convert traditional IRA or 401(k) balances to Roth at the 10%, 12%, or 22% bracket. This is significantly cheaper than the 32% or 37% rate your heirs might pay on inherited traditional IRA distributions.

Sources indicate that review your estate plan every three years at minimum and immediately after any major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary, significant change in net worth, or a move to a newly introduced state. Early retirees have a longer planning horizon, making regular updates even more key than for conventional retirees.

It has been revealed that estate planning for early retirees is not a modified version of conventional retirement planning — it is a fundamentally different discipline. You face a longer incapacity window, a bigger healthcare gap, more exposure to tax law changes, and decades of asset protection needs. The FIRE community excels at building wealth through savings rate optimization and investment discipline. Apply that same rigor to your estate strategy: execute foundational documents before leaving your job, optimize beneficiary designations for the SECURE Act, pursue Roth conversions during low-income years, and protect your assets with umbrella insurance and trust structures. The wealth you built deserves a plan that survives as long as your retirement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

So what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions? Is there really any noticeable difference between carets, chevrons, arrows, and triangles?

It has been revealed that well, research shows that there is some difference indeed. But what’s more interesting is that split menus are harmful, why it’s better to not have icons and text labels link to different actions, and why the caret is the safest icon choice. Let’s dive in!

It has been revealed that the findings aren’t very surprising: without any icon in use, users expect that tapping on the menu item would take them directly to a new page. Users often struggle with custom icons as they don’t clearly signal that they’ll open an accordion. And people tend to tap fairly equally on the icon and on the label for most icons.

It has been revealed that many designs (like the one below) tend to slightly overcomplicate things by adding arrows and carets pointing everywhere, depending on the state of the accordion. But typically we don’t need to use an arrow to indicate a link to the category.

The rule of thumb is very simple: if it’s a link, the easiest and most effective way is to simply underline it — without any arrow, caret, or other icon. Perhaps it’s not particularly exciting, but it works flawlessly every single time.

Sources indicate that using a right-facing arrow icon ▶ isn’t associated with an expectation of going directly to a new page. And having the same icon pointing down ▼ doesn’t necessarily imply that an accordion is going to open on tap/click.

It’s a good idea to avoid split buttons for accordions — where the text label links directly to a page, but the icon opens the accordion. Instead, it’s much more reliable to allow users to tap on a main category and expose the menu; and to access the category page, we add a link to it inside the menu.

In a recent development, for accordions, we typically use +/− or arrows ↓/↑ to signal expanded and collapsed states, and typically it works well. However, both have many different interpretations. Plus + can mean anything from saving for later to adding to cart to zooming in, and can be particularly confusing for multi-level navigation, with many levels open at the same time.

Recent findings suggest that arrows ↓/↑ can mean scrolling or sliding or finding the next match, but also a jump to a particular portion of a page. Both plus and arrows are well-understood and work, but depending on the design, can be confusing — mostly because they are overloaded.

Industry observers note that the safe choice is to use the caret/triangle pointing down ▼ by default, and change it to a caret pointing up or a caret pointing sideways ▶ on interaction. If you need an alternative, then +/- typically work well, too.

But we certainly don’t need any further icons or arrows to indicate where the links go. The same goes for split menus, which often produce more mistakes than help. Instead, we have one button or dropdown that does exactly one thing — demonstrates all options and allows customers to drill down.

Recent findings suggest that and if you need a direct link, we link the title directly to the page and underline it. More often than not, simpler is better.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The first thing you see is the space between the letters.
  • Johnson Banks started from a Philip Johnson line, that all great architecture is the design of space that contains, cuddles, exalts, or stimulates the people in that space, and let the negative space inside the four letters carry the idea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Johnson Banks rebuilds RIBA for its 200th birthday: the RIBA brand identity turns negative space into a bold typographic mark.

The first thing you see is the space between the letters. RIBA arrives as four solid capitals on a pale wall, each letter built from the gaps around it, the R split into a bowl and a leg, the B into two stacked bowls, the A into a triangle over a flat base. It is a mark about architecture made from architecture itself, walls and openings rather than a drawn symbol, and it holds at every size, from a tote bag to a building banner.

The type does the work. Johnson Banks started from a Philip Johnson line, that all great architecture is the design of space that contains, cuddles, exalts, or stimulates the people in that space, and let the negative space inside the four letters carry the idea. The mark can sit on top of a photograph, cut into it, or anchor a corner or an edge, and the same logic runs through a set of drop capitals, letters drawn to open a page like a doorway.

The old identity, letters drawn by Eric Gill beside a highly detailed symbol, had drifted over twenty-five years into hundreds of sub-brands with no house style holding them together. The new system pulls them back into line, with related identities for RSAW, the Royal Society of Architects in Wales, and RIBAJ, the institute journal, each sitting inside the same approach, and clear guidelines built on accessible fonts so the brand stays useful and durable.

Colour went back to the beginning. The historic red, the shade the public knows from RIBA signboards, returns front and centre, running across the tote bag, the drawing stencil and the vertical banner on a brick facade. Against it, the palette stays quiet, stone grey, pale blue, black, so the red reads as a signal rather than a decoration, and the crest, the two lions, survives in a simplified, softened form as a quiet sign-off, debossed in black on black.

It has been revealed that the system proves itself on the objects architects use. Book spines carry RIBA, RSAW and RIBAJ in red, white and blue on a wooden shelf. A red stencil ruler cuts the letters into a drawing tool. A poster for the Domestic Building Contract pairs a giant yellow D with a red architectural photograph. And the illustration style, flat geometric shapes in red, blue and green with small cut-out figures, gives the brand a way to talk about people without a photograph.
