📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Studio operations software Programa has redesigned its programme to rethink how interior design studios operate, giving practices more flexibility and freeing up their time.

According to Programa, beautiful interiors are built on “hundreds of decisions”, which take long periods of time to decide upon and upgrade across multiple spreadsheets.

Each decision brings specification details, quantities, pricing and revisions that studios must keep updated as a project develops.

These include minute, precise details such as dimensions, materials, finishes, technical requirements, and component quantities.

Programa‘s redesigned programme keeps a record of each item used in an interior project, from furniture and lighting to hardware and finishes, and optimises their organisation based on how the project runs.

The organization explained that increased AI use is making convincing images “easier to generate than ever”, yet clients often run into logistical issues when using this alone.

For example, the AI model doesn’t take into account whether a wardrobe or sofa fits through the door, suits the needs of the people living there, or whether the overall design takes full advantage of a space’s natural light.

With Programa, the designer can smoothly make these judgements using the software’s organisation of specifications, cost, quantities and overall project coordination.

The company explained that if a designer updates a product’s shared specification once, the change appears in the Programa schedules that include it, while quantities can be individually allocated by room.

For Austin Carrier of Californian design studio, Hommeboys Interiors, this is particularly helpful.

“We use schedules for everything from lighting and hardware to plumbing fixtures and furniture, indoor and outdoor,” Carrier explained.

“For furniture, we can break down every room, then the pieces within that room, and give clients several options to reject or accept,” he added.

According to recent reports, as a result, the software aims to cut the “gruelling amount of work” updating schedules, preparing presentations, and communicating with suppliers. It also reduces repeated data entry, freeing up time.

The platform is defined as an “alternative to spreadsheets”, which often have to be made from scratch and reformatted for different presentations.

“The matter with the spreadsheet is that it’s like a blank cell,” added Los Angeles-based designer Paul Chan. “You can put anything in there – it doesn’t carry from one project to another.”.

In a recent development, “With Programa, I can take a format from one project and move it into the next,” Chan continued. “There’s consistency between each project.”.

Specifically, the Programa Schedule function details the items’ code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.

It offers a streamlined place to reference drawings, get client approval and work with contractors to meet on-site deadlines.

The company explained that one of its platform’s main benefits is that it can be used from early product decision-making through to final delivery.

Here, the studio manages the specification and controls what is shared, whereas the clients review selections and provide approvals. Collaborators also receive the information relevant to their work.

“Once we get all of the information in there, we can send it out in one email to all of our vendors, and then they are able to get us pricing back very easily,” added Tana Nesbitt-Hayes of Studio 8 Architect.

“If we’re exceeding our budget in one area, we can tailor it back. It’s always up-to-date.”.

Sources indicate that “We share our Programa Schedules with the millworkers and the engineers,” she added. “They can see the refrigerator we’re going to put in, and they can make the panels to fit.”.

Programa offers a free trial for all studios. To learn more, visit its website.

Latest Update: Seaweed earplug among grant-winning Design Museum prototypes

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A single-use earplug crafted from seaweed, two plant-based insulation materials and a homegrown timber kit-of-parts for low-rise buildings are among the projects that have been awarded Design Museum grants.
  • UK-based studios Searo Labs, WeCanMake, Local Works Studio and SY Ecofit have been granted a share of £280,000 from the Design Museum for their “cutting-edge” environmental prototypes.
  • Described as the “world’s first seaweed-based single-use earplug”, SearoSoft by Cambridge-based Searo Labs is a fully biodegradable and renewable alternative to single-use earplugs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A single-use earplug crafted from seaweed, two plant-based insulation materials and a homegrown timber kit-of-parts for low-rise buildings are among the projects that have been awarded Design Museum grants.

UK-based studios Searo Labs, WeCanMake, Local Works Studio and SY Ecofit have been granted a share of £280,000 from the Design Museum for their “cutting-edge” environmental prototypes.

Described as the “world’s first seaweed-based single-use earplug”, SearoSoft by Cambridge-based Searo Labs is a fully biodegradable and renewable alternative to single-use earplugs.

According to SearoSoft, the soft, mouldable earplugs are made without microplastics or chemicals and designed to hydrate the ear canal, unlike plastic-based products, which can be drying.

Once discarded, they are biodegradable in water or soil after 30 days. As seaweed is a regenerative crop, SearoSoft explained that there is no need for land, freshwater or fertilisers, making the process simple and more sustainable.

Sources indicate that among the other prototypes is a building material project by Sussex-based Local Works Studio. The initiative, named Ferment, will repurpose agricultural waste into an insulating material fit for retrofitting buildings.

Local Works Studio aims to develop an accessible product for farms via what it calls a “harvest-to-house system”, where farmers can produce the insulation themselves using their existing infrastructure, skills and machinery.

Bristol-based studio WeCanMake’s winning prototype, Neighbourhood Factory Futures, is a homegrown timber kit-of-parts system designed to be used for constructing low-rise apartment buildings.

With the Design Museum’s grant, the studio intends to create a neighbourhood factory model, allowing local communities to build and maintain their own homes.

WeCanMake explained it created the system as part of a wider movement aiming to make the UK a “nation of growers, producers and makers” while using reusable materials that store, rather than emit, carbon.

Prototyping PhytoFloc by social enterprise SY Ecofit in collaboration with Phyona and Studio Bio is a zero-waste project that, similarly to Local Works Studio, aims to develop plant-based insulation for building construction.

The project uses biowaste created as a byproduct of phytomining, where former industrial land is rejuvenated by plants that extract pollutants from the soil.

The project intends to recognise the value of post-industrial soils while creating a locally made, low-carbon material.

The grants are part of the Design Museum’s Future Observatory program, which is run in partnership with the Arts and Humanities Research Council. The winning projects were amongst 140 prototypes that were submitted to the scheme.

The museum explained that at a time when supply chains are under pressure, the Future Observatory aims to support designers’ practical research to drive the green transition.

“The climate crisis demands rapid change, and we believe that design is critically vital if we are to meet that challenge,” remarked Design Museum director Tim Marlow.

“The presence of Future Observatory allows us an extraordinary opportunity to get involved with practitioners and problem-solvers and have a direct impact on the development of new technologies at the frontier of current design thinking.”.

The four projects will be funded from November 2026 until July 2027. Afterwards, the prototypes will be tested and begin the commercialisation process.

#115293. Latest Update: Abu Dhabi markets itself to global elites—can its public art biennial reach local communities?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1030 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Abu Dhabi markets itself to global elites—can its public art biennial reach local communities?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The arrival of Frieze furthers Abu Dhabi’s ambitions to become a premier events destination for global elites.
  • Recent findings suggest that but a glittering trail of franchised events is unlikely to leave a lasting impact on the local communities that have built Abu Dhabi and will continue to sustain it.
  • Sources indicate that public art appears to be one strategy, so proposes the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial (until 15 February 2027).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The arrival of Frieze furthers Abu Dhabi’s ambitions to become a premier events destination for global elites. Beyond the fair (which runs until 22 November), the coming weeks will see the jetset descend on the emirate to bid on Picassos at Sotheby’s, sit front row at the Grand Prix and Abu Dhabi Open tournaments, and rub shoulders with celebrities and chief executives at the Global Cultural Forum and the Milken Institute's Middle East and Africa Summit.

Recent findings suggest that but a glittering trail of franchised events is unlikely to leave a lasting impact on the local communities that have built Abu Dhabi and will continue to sustain it. Focusing efforts on attracting the itinerant super-rich might also prove short-sighted for a country surrounded by well-armed and hostile neighbours. So, how to engage those who will remain when regional conflicts escalate or the markets turn?

Sources indicate that public art appears to be one strategy, so proposes the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial (until 15 February 2027). Organised by the Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT), the exhibition Home: A Glossary for a Communal Sense of Place has brought 18 works—most of them fresh commissions—to public sites across the city, with a further four situated in the nearby oasis desert town of Al Ain.

Asunción Molinos Gordo, Bil Hana wa Al Afia (2026), installation view, Al Ain.Image courtesy of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Department of Culture and Tourism— Abu Dhabi.

“Everyday life is central” to this biennial “both as backdrop and method”, writes its artistic director, Elvira Dyangani Ose, in the accompanying guide. Out in the desert, Iron Age irrigation systems still used today form the basis of Ascunción Molinos Gordo’s rammed earth sculpture Bil Hana wa Al Afia (2026), installed among working farms during the biennial’s run. Back in the city, the ubiquitous infrastructure of cooling vents is brought to the fore by Shama Al Hamed’s installation of fluorescent aluminium ducting, which spill out like entrails from the observation deck of the former industrial port.

In a recent development, key to a public art biennial concerned with the quotidian is appealing to non-art specialist audiences. This means considering the “many publics” that exist in Abu Dhabi, Dyangani Ose says. Visitors at sunset will see families jumping on Ivan Argote’s see-saw installation and zooming down its animal-shaped slides.

In a recent development, despite the temporary nature of an exhibition, each edition of the biennial achieves permanence through its acquisition structure. Last edition, 15 works—around half—were acquired by Public Art Abu Dhabi and are now on display across the city. They include a crescent of silver oyster sculptures by the Emirati artist Farah Al Qasimi, referencing the Arabian Gulf’s once-booming pearl diving industry.

Sources indicate that the director of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Clémence Bergal, indicates a similar acquisition round will take place at the end of this edition. “With so many of the biennial’s works being new commissions, it is a great way to collect work that feels deeply connected and responsive to Abu Dhabi,” she says.

Elvira Dyangani Ose, artistic director of the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial.

Industry observers note that the biennial is not only a tool for engaging Abu Dhabi’s various communities, but for considering how they live with each other. The theme of this year is the unstable and contested definition of “home”, and Dyangani Ose writes in the catalogue that she is interested in how a “communal sense of place” is formed and negotiated by various groups, sometimes of vastly different cultures and material conditions. “Abu Dhabi is a city in which that distinction matters enormously,” she writes. “Communities from across the world share its streets, its coastline, its daily rhythms without sharing the same histories, the same rights or the same relationship to the land.”.

The curatorial statement provides a potent line of inquiry in a country where only a small portion of the population—estimated to be around 12%—has citizenship, and in which the working and living conditions of migrant labourers has been criticised by leading human rights organisations.

Recent findings suggest that these complications appear to be broached obliquely in the multiple references to migration and labour throughout the biennial, including in a striking coastline installation by the Ghanaian artist Serge Attukwei Clottey, composed of thousands of interlocking yellow plastic pieces made from Kuffuor gallons—containers that are ubiquitous in Accra and used to transport cooking oil, water and fuel. These Kuffuor installations are Clottey’s signature, and he has spoken widely about how they refer, in part, to the imbalanced relations of labour and resource extraction between African nations and their trading partners. The UAE is Ghana’s third-most notable importer, chiefly purchasing gold. Immigrants from Ghana and other West African nations represent an increasingly large portion of the UAE's manual labour force, chiefly working in construction, hospitality and security services.

Yinka Shonibare, Wind Sculpture (TG) III (2026), installationview, Abu Dhabi, 2026.

Image courtesy of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Department of Culture and Tourism— Abu Dhabi.

Unsurprisingly considering the emirate's strict censorship laws, little in the show could be openly perceived as critical, at least of the UAE. Dyangani Ose tells The Art Newspaper that there are certain “limits presented by the framework” of a publicly funded exhibition in Abu Dhabi. She adds that "as global subjects", we are all bound within certain limits.

According to recent reports, to its credit, the biennial's public setting provides opportunities for conversations that many art institutions in other parts of the world might shy away from. For instance, Yinka Shonibare’s towering metal plume, painted in both his signature Dutch wax patterns and those of Bedouin textiles, serves as a welcome shade structure for outdoor labourers working in the harsh midday sun. "These publics are just as crucial to take into account as any other," Dyangani Ose indicates.

It has been revealed that indeed, providing a platform for a diverse and unexpected set of interactions is a vital part of how Dyangani Ose conceives of a communal sense of place, as “making meaning, despite differences, in public”. For the biennial, this might be its greatest impact of all.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Images courtesy of Waugh Thistleton Architects.
  • UK studio Waugh Thistleton Architects is set to transform the Edwardian Westbrook Pavilion in Margate, UK, into an arts centre for British artist Tracey Emin with a cafe, public sauna and changing rooms.
  • “The project will bring a much-loved seafront building back into use, combining its original purpose with new spaces for art, culture and the local community,” said Waugh Thistleton Architects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Waugh Thistleton Architects.

UK studio Waugh Thistleton Architects is set to transform the Edwardian Westbrook Pavilion in Margate, UK, into an arts centre for British artist Tracey Emin with a cafe, public sauna and changing rooms.

“The project will bring a much-loved seafront building back into use, combining its original purpose with new spaces for art, culture and the local community,” said Waugh Thistleton Architects.

The studio recently won planning permission from the local council to convert the abandoned building, which Emin purchased in 2023, into a facility run by the Tracey Emin Foundation.

The project aims to return the building to its former use as a changing room for swimmers and as a tea room, when it originally opened in 1914.

“Originally opened in 1914, the building provided public changing facilities for sea-bathing and a tea room,” stated the studio.

“Following storm damage in the Great North Sea Storm of 1953, subsequent alterations detracted from its original Edwardian character,” it continued.

“The renovated pavilion will accommodate artist studios, an art gallery, clubroom, cafe, sea-bathing changing facilities, a fresh sauna and refurbished public toilets, restoring its original role as a place for bathing and socialising by the sea.”.

Recent findings suggest that along with making the pavilion a building used by the public again, the studio aims to return the building’s core to its Edwardian look by removing later additions. It will also add glazed facades to the wings on either side of the central pavilion.

The building will be topped by a rooftop terrace, while a public toilet on the site will be renovated.

“The design draws on the proportions and character of the original building, removing later additions and reinstating lost features such as the historic belvederes which top the central tower structures,” remarked the studio.

“The beachfront facade will see a new glazing system and colonnade to each of the building’s wings, with a new sheltered archway forming a new seating terrace at the building’s heart,” it continued.

“The design seeks to reference the original architecture while providing contemporary needs of a public building. Where original features are references, these are distinguishable architecturally.”.

Emin is one of the UK’s best-known living artists. We recently produced a video of a landmark exhibition of her work at Tate Modern.

Recent projects by Waugh Thistleton Architects include prepares for the “tallest mass timber office building in the US”.

Images courtesy of Waugh Thistleton Architects.

Breaking: Cara de Vaca Brand Identity Is a Masterclass in Branding

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anagrama builds the Cara de Vaca brand identity from Monterrey market signs, a custom typeface, and posters that shout in black and orange.
  • Cara de Vaca is a Monterrey restaurant built on fire cooking, natural wine, and classic drinks.
  • The logo mixes fonts the way a shop owner mixes lettering on a hand-painted sign, and that looseness is the point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anagrama builds the Cara de Vaca brand identity from Monterrey market signs, a custom typeface, and posters that shout in black and orange.

Cara de Vaca is a Monterrey restaurant built on fire cooking, natural wine, and classic drinks. Chef Chuy Villarreal cooks regional cuisine as an evolution of the Regiomontana barbecue, and Anagrama answers with a system borrowed from the hand-painted business signs of downtown Monterrey. Black fields carry the shouting, orange paper carries the warmth, and a smiling face and a small cow sit beside the wordmark like a stamp.

The logo mixes fonts the way a shop owner mixes lettering on a hand-painted sign, and that looseness is the point. Anagrama drew a custom typeface, Lechon Sans, from the same source, built for social media lockups that spotlight a single word. The specimen shows the full set: capitals, numerals, punctuation, arrows, and small symbols that include the smiley face, the cow, and a pig.

According to recent reports, the lockups take their cues from Mercado Juarez, the downtown market where the studio photographed signs to dress the restaurant walls. Phrases stack in mixed sizes with quotation marks doing the work of a frame: BARBACOA, LECHON, CABRITO. VINOS NATURALES, BIEN FRIOS. GRAN DOMINGO. A word goes huge when it matters, small when it is a wink, and the quotes and rules hold the pieces together.

The posters are physical objects first. One orange sheet curls at the corner against a black field, its type running diagonally across the page. A kraft sheet carries the same treatment, the paper grain showing through the ink. The black behind both does quiet work: it makes the orange and the kraft read as light in a dark room.

The system spreads across everything a guest can hold. Tote bags run in cream, green, and orange, each carrying a different phrase, and a yellow cattle ear tag hangs from the handles as the label. Business cards take the same marks in gold foil, the cow and the smiley pressed small into white stock.

Sources indicate that inside the restaurant the identity turns architectural. A neon CARA DE VACA sign glows red over the entrance at night: the logo lettering, now in light. Wood and metal frame the room, brand marks sit on walls and mirrors, and plants soften the space around the central bar, where natural wines and Mexican distillates pour.

The website carries the same voice, quieter: the personality, the menu photos, a reservation button, and the address. Social posts use the lockups the typeface was built for, phrases set large enough to read at a scroll. From a neon sign to a phone screen, the identity never changes its register.

See more from Anagrama on their website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects.

A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.

The church will occupy a at the moment underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban’s signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.

According to Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci, the overarching goal is for the church to help establish a greater sense of community and place in the area, which they describe as having a “fragmented urban fabric”.

“We wanted to design a place of worship that also brings the whole community together,” stated Ban.

“The timber structure expresses the idea of a tent, a simple, welcoming form that connects people with one another and with their surroundings. Through this project, we hope architecture can help create a new sense of belonging in the neighbourhood.”.

Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci’s proposal was the winning entry of a competition for the church.

It is one of five winning designs selected as part of the Upcoming Churches Programme – an initiative led by the local church district, the Diocese of Rome, and the Italian Episcopal Conference, an assembly of Catholic bishops, to provide permanent homes for parish communities in the region.

As part of the project, four fresh churches will be built, while one existing parish complex will be extended.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be built on a raised public plaza, with various parish facilities, community spaces and a priest’s residence embedded below.

In a recent development, its key feature will be its angular roof, which is shaped like a cross but not immediately readable as one. This is modelled on a latent cross – a feature in sacred architecture, in which a cross shape is integrated in the spatial design, without being clearly visible.

According to recent reports, inside, the church will have a diamond-shaped strategy, with large stained-glass windows positioned in the four cardinal directions. They will be triangular in shape and feature designs modelled on neighbourhood street art.

The project will be complete with a landscaped park, as well as various recreational and sports facilities, which the studios noted will “create opportunities for social interaction and everyday activities”.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex is not the first church project by Ban. Among his others is the landmark Cardboard Cathedral in Fresh Zealand, which is formed of 98 cardboard tubes combined with wood and polycarbonate. We named it the most significant building of 2013 in our list of the 25 most significant buildings of the 21st century.

Other Italian church proposals recently featured on Dezeen include Stefano Boeri Architetti’s design for the Ambrosian Monastery in Milan, which will have a sail-like roof form.

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects.

In a recent development, imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji. Or picture arriving at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where Haussmann architecture frames your every view and the concierge greets you by name. Or standing in the Park Hyatt New York, 25 floors above Midtown, watching the city sprawl in every direction from a room that costs more per night than most people's monthly car payment. Now imagine paying nearly nothing for it. That's the power of the World of Hyatt award chart — and the Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community's collective jaw drop: a single night at the Park Hyatt New York regularly retails for **$1,200–$2,000**. The Park Hyatt Tokyo commands **$800–$1,500** per night. The Park Hyatt Paris? Easily **$1,000+** in peak seasons. Yet every one of these properties sits at **Category 7**, bookable for just **25,000–30,000 World of Hyatt points** per night. At 30,000 points for a $1,500 room, you're extracting **5 cents per point (cpp)** — in a world where most loyalty programs are engineered to deliver 1–1.5 cpp if you're lucky. The CPP range for this sweet spot runs from **2.7 cpp all the way to 6.7 cpp**, meaning even a modest redemption delivers 2–3x the value of a typical points transaction. Why does this gap exist? Because Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** anchored to categories, not real-time cash pricing. When demand spikes — New Year's Eve in New York, cherry blossom season in Tokyo, Paris Fashion Week — cash rates explode upward while your points cost stays locked. The hotel's revenue management team can't touch your award rate. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community is built to exploit. This isn't aspirational travel for the ultra-wealthy. This is FI-minded travel: understanding the system, earning points intentionally, and converting them into experiences that would otherwise require an extra year of saving. A two-night stay at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for 60,000 points — points you can earn from a single credit card welcome bonus — is the kind of redemption that reframes what financial independence actually looks like in practice.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.

In a recent development, here's how the Hyatt award chart works: properties are assigned to Categories 1 through 8, with standard award nights running from 3,500 points (Cat 1) up to 45,000 points (Cat 8). Park Hyatt properties — the absolute pinnacle of the Hyatt portfolio, a collection of ultra-luxury city hotels that competes directly with Four Seasons and Ritz-Carlton — fall predominantly into Category 7 (25,000 points/night) and Category 8 (40,000 points/night). But unlike Four Seasons or Ritz-Carlton, which have largely abandoned fixed award charts in favor of dynamic pricing that tracks cash rates, Hyatt has held the line on fixed pricing. This is a rare and increasingly endangered feature in hotel loyalty, which is exactly why the ChooseFI community should be actively using it now.

Industry observers note that the transfer path that makes this accessible is Chase Ultimate Rewards. Chase transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant — meaning you can spot availability, transfer your points, and book within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, also instantly, giving you two powerful earning pipelines into the same program.

This matters enormously for strategy. Chase Ultimate Rewards is arguably the most flexible points currency in travel rewards — earned through cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve — and the fact that it flows directly into Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio without any degradation is a genuine gift. 30,000 Chase UR points become exactly 30,000 Hyatt points. No conversion fees, no waiting period, no surprises.

Recent findings suggest that another critical mechanism: World of Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award redemptions. With hotel awards this is less of an issue than with airline programs, but it reflects Hyatt's broader philosophy of clean, predictable award pricing. What you see is what you pay — taxes and fees on hotel awards are typically minimal.

Now layer in Globalist status, and the value compounds further. World of Hyatt's top-tier elite status (earned at 60 qualifying nights per year) unlocks complimentary suite upgrades at check-in (space available) and free breakfast for two guests daily. If you're a Globalist checking into the Park Hyatt New York and you receive a suite upgrade, you've just added hundreds of dollars of daily value to an already exceptional redemption — and free breakfast at a Park Hyatt can easily run $60–$90 per person.

The booking window is 395 days out, which matters for high-demand dates. The Park Hyatt Tokyo during cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or the Park Hyatt Upcoming York around major events will see award availability evaporate swiftly. Understanding that you can search and book nearly 13 months in advance is your single biggest tactical advantage for locking in prime dates.

Recent findings suggest that finally, it's worth understanding what you're getting at the property level. Park Hyatt is not Hyatt Regency or even Andaz — it's Hyatt's true ultra-luxury tier, with butler service, marble bathrooms, curated art collections, and some of the best city-view room designs in the world. The points-to-experience ratio here is genuinely exceptional.

Recent findings suggest that search flexibly. If your first-choice dates show no availability, shift by a day or two — award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is released in small blocks and replenished irregularly. Use the calendar view to scan multiple dates at once.

This is where most people hit a wall — they discover the sweet spot, feel excited, and then find no availability for their dates. **Three tips to overcome the availability challenge:** 1. **Use the full 395-day booking window.** Plan further ahead than feels natural. Tech Report: International photography museum Fotografiska opens in Shenzhen

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The international photography museum Fotografiska has recently launched in Shenzhen, its second space in mainland China, after Fotografiska Shanghai opened in 2023.
  • The organisation, founded in Stockholm in 2010, also currently has locations in the Swedish capital, Latest York, Berlin and Tallinn; and a new venue, in Oslo, is scheduled to open in 2028.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Museum-going culture [in Shenzhen] isn’t as deeply entrenched as it is in Shanghai or Hong Kong,” Devillers claims, and its art-going demographic skews heavily toward young families and professionals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The international photography museum Fotografiska has recently launched in Shenzhen, its second space in mainland China, after Fotografiska Shanghai opened in 2023. “The strategy was always to self-fund the first space in Shanghai, and then expand through strategic partnerships for subsequent locations,” says Christian Devillers, the managing director for Fotografiska China.

The organisation, founded in Stockholm in 2010, also currently has locations in the Swedish capital, Latest York, Berlin and Tallinn; and a new venue, in Oslo, is scheduled to open in 2028.

Recent findings suggest that “Museum-going culture [in Shenzhen] isn’t as deeply entrenched as it is in Shanghai or Hong Kong,” Devillers claims, and its art-going demographic skews heavily toward young families and professionals. Fotografiska Shenzhen is replicating Shanghai’s late hours and lifestyle offerings, which draw office workers commuting to the city centres, and its first public day on the 1 October national holiday drew more than 1,000 paying visitors.

Sources indicate that the project opened with exhibitions across the 5,300 sq. m facility, including a Shi Guowei solo show and Toiletpaper, showcasing Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari’s titular magazine (both until 14 March 2027). They have joined a show of photography award Prix Pictet (until 29 November), the six-artist group show Transcendent Realities (until 1 October 2027) and a Michael Najjar solo exhibition (until 17 January 2027). Subsequent planned events include a show of Hong Kong photographers featuring, among others, Ho Fan (1931-2016).

In Shanghai, even with Fotografiska’s busy traffic, admissions and memberships account for only around 20% of total revenue, Devillers notes. The museum instead depends on commercial partnerships, and retail and food and drink sales. Fotografiska Shenzhen’s six-year partnership agreement with landlord China Resources Land aims to draw a profit by year three. The institution has set an initial target of 70,000 visitors for 2027.

Fotografiska Shenzhen is located in the upscale retail complex Shenzhen Bay MixC, which is also home to a new immersive art concept called Base. They join several new and forthcoming cultural projects in the city, which is making a concerted push to raise its artistic profile, such as the recently-opened Shenzhen International Art Museum and Shenzhen Bay Cultural Plaza. This month will also see the long-running Hong Kong fair Fine Art Asia relocate to the mainland city (26-29 November).

Breaking: Meet Swedish Girls, Sabine Marcelis’s pick for Dezeen's 20x20 project

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler. In this interview, we learn why the design duo deliberately play into stereotypes.

The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.

“I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.

Josefin Zachrisson and Mira Bergh run multidisciplinary studio Swedish Girls between Stockholm and Milan, creating furniture, installations and set design.

In a recent development, the duo met during their studies at Sweden’s Beckmans College of Design, where they graduated in 2019. They bonded over a desire to make work “without hierarchies” and maintain creative control of the studio’s output, which they prefer to call their ever-expanding “universe”.

The Big Bang for Swedish Girls was the selection of their collective’s tongue-in-cheek name, chosen after their first exhibition outing at Milan design week.

For experimental platform Alcova in 2021, Zachrisson and Bergh unveiled their ongoing metal rod Seats System project (pictured left).

Originally a single piece of modular seating without a defined front or back, the project has evolved into more metal pieces that follow the same design language, including a fruit bowl and a candle holder.

“We overheard people talking about our furniture, asking who made it, and others were like, ‘ah, it was those Swedish girls’, and we felt a bit belittled by it,” recalled Zachrisson. The duo had previously made work under their own names.

Sources indicate that “The Swedish girl has obviously become a phenomenon,” added Bergh. “You know, blonde, sexy. But when we were talking about it, we also found it really funny because it’s so stereotypical. We thought we’d call ourselves Swedish Girls because everybody else was already calling us that.”.

Sources indicate that humour is intrinsic to Zachrisson and Bergh’s interdisciplinary practice. Even their website, admired by Marcelis, was playfully designed as a Swedish Girls-branded Google search engine. It is meant to look like the internet itself, complete with mock web pages listing each of the collective’s projects.

“We got the idea when we launched the name Swedish Girls,” the pair explained.

“A professor from Beckmans called and said that we should change our name because when she Googled ‘Swedish Girls’, the search result was not exactly art and design,” they added.

“We thought that was so funny and decided to make Google about us instead of changing our name.”.

Another of the duo’s wit-inflected projects is Only Fans, an installation presented at Gothenburg’s Röhsska design museum in 2024 during local music festival Way Out West.

Dubbed “a multidimensional art experience about fan culture” in all its forms, the installation included 25 electric fans, selected as a riff on adult content platform OnlyFans, where women are often the subject of scrutiny.

“The installation was interactive, so that visitors could stand in the middle of the fans in a hysterical storm,” noted Bergh.

It has been revealed that our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things. But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life.

Alongside the fans, the collective presented seven laser-cut steel chairs emblazoned with I <3 Swedish Girls, along with a fanzine and female mannequins wearing “metal merch” designed by Zachrisson and Bergh.

“Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things,” considered Zachrisson.

“But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life,” she continued. “It feels like a way to approach it that makes it accessible.”.

“Sometimes it’s hard because we get these questions like, ‘are you a feminist?'” added the designer. “But it’s inherently political to be a woman moving through the world. Our work is just reacting to our reality.”.

The pair is keen to highlight that although they make furniture, “social values are always a starting point” for their projects.

“We really want to have a practice that feels purposeful,” said Zachrisson, considering the significance of partnering with institutions like design museums.

“We’ve realised that showing work in public spaces is the most important thing,” she continued.

Recent findings suggest that “Especially because the materials and processes we use have become quite expensive. So we want to put our pieces in public spaces so that everyone can take part in some way.”.

“You meet all different kinds of people, and we talk to them and grow from it,” added Bergh.

The hardest thing is to earn money. We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money.

Despite Swedish Girls’ various collaborations and recurring presence at Milan design week, seven years after leaving Beckmans, Bergh and Zachrisson continue to work in cafes and supermarkets to fund their design practice.

The duo are hyperaware of the difficulties faced by emerging creatives, especially those like themselves who, as they put it, “want to listen to your gut and be close to the process”.

Industry observers note that “The hardest thing is to earn money,” said Bergh. “We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money on very quick timelines. I feel like we should have more respect.”.

“You don’t get paid in a way where you as two people can survive,” added Zachrisson. “But all these years of working and keeping our creative integrity is paying off in every way except financially.”.

When it comes to building their studio, the designers consider themselves to be playing the long game.

“Long term, it’s an investment to do it this way because we have now created a context where we can feel freedom and gain respect, which is why we were so happy when Sabine nominated us,” remarked Zachrisson.

“You can measure success in so many different ways and with this we feel respected, and that is so valuable.”.

The duo noted funding that they won from Sweden’s Konstnärsnämnden arts council after graduating gave them a significant leg up when they were just starting out.

Zachrisson and Bergh are concerned that scholarships like theirs have been scarcer across Sweden in recent years thanks to the country’s right-wing administration, which came into power in 2022 and has only just been voted out of office.

Recent findings suggest that “All the artists we have talked to have felt an extreme difference in that time,” noted Zachrisson. “The share of the total budget allocated to culture has not been this low in 26 years.”.

Still, the pair are confident and excited about what’s to come.

Industry observers note that “It comes in handy that we have a broad practice,” said Bergh. “We have plans for the future to make it easier for ourselves to be designers.”.

According to recent reports, “I like how they surprise with their projects and feel like we have only seen chapter one of their story,” concluded Marcelis. “And I can’t wait to discover the next chapter.”.

Tiger Dingsunâs portfolio web design opens on scattered collage stacks before clearing into a crisp four-column index of projects and drafts.

In a recent development, opening tiger.exposed feels like stepping up to a studio desk buried under loose prints, sketches, and half-sorted notes. As Hover States puts it, the site moves from scattered stacks to an orderly list, exposing both personality and practice. Two oversized graphic piles land directly over the viewport. On the left, a stark black-and-white brush creature maps opposing ideas like light and darkness beside poison and antidote; on the right, a hand-drawn rainbow frog spirals over a shell collage. Deeper layers reveal stamp-sheet conceptual grids, pixel registration marks, and glowing lizards crossing a cloudy sky. It isnât decoration. Tiny print slivers peek along all four edges, hinting that an archive waits underneath.

Clearing the stacks flips the whole mood. A bare white canvas takes over, split into four tight columns of black sans-serif titles ruled by crisp horizontal hairlines. Tiger Dingsun sorts the work into Web, Graphic Design, Writing, and Type Design with zero drop-down chrome or bulky thumbnails. Entries like Heavy Traffic Magazine, Reading Machines, Rhizome 7x7 2026, and Wyvern Sans (work-in-progress) read like a working ledger. Hovering over a line like The End is Not the End dims the type softly to confirm focus. Still, the web design doesnât lose its opening humor â a tiny orange brick-built figure sits tucked in the lower-right corner.

Clicking any title proves the index isnât just a splash screen. Selecting FWB Fest '25 Poster shifts the ruled list into a persistent right-hand rail while a wide left pane displays the work. Two finished posters labeled final (light) and final (dark) sit side by side, followed right below by numbered iterations marked draft 3 through draft 6. Putting early studies beside finished prints makes this web design feel candid about how graphic work actually takes shape. Even the brief bio above the gallery stays plain-spoken, listing talks at Parsons, SVA, and Rhizome next to a direct email note. Thereâs no heavy agency shell here, only a clean switch between messy curiosity and sharp filing.
